speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion concerning an important and urgent matter.
To prevent the diverging constitutional positions which are now being expressed on the future of our country from bringing forth government decisions that could be contrary to the financial interests of the people of Quebec, and given the statements of certain ministers and the right hon. That the federal government give Quebec an amount equivalent to the investment it would refuse to make on the territory of that province.

The federal government will introduce within a month a working paper dealing with the problems and methods of dumping the wage and price control program.
Robert Kaplan, parliamentary secretary to Finance minister Donald Macdonald, revealed the existence of the paper last night while speaking at a Hamilton Mountain riding association meeting.
In an interview after the meeting Kaplan was reluctant to discuss details of the paper, saying he could not speak for Macdonald.
But he said details of the document, an official federal government green paper, will be discussed at a federal and provincial finance ministers conference scheduled for May 4.
Kaplan said the federal government set tough goals with the anti-inflation program and now has reached these goals but must find a satisfactory way out of controls.
"We want to get back to a free market system" he said. "The challenge is to find a way out of controls that won't make inflation soar and wages increase as they did before controls."
He referred to the government paper as a "de-control program" and said it is the one the federal government sees in use in the post-control period.
While Kaplan would not discuss how the plan was devised, it follows a series of tripartite meetings between Prime Minister Trudeau, top cabinet ministers, labour and business leaders. Those meetings were followed by renewed demands from business and labour for a quick end to control.
Am I not allowed, Mr. Speaker, to ask the Minister of Finance about a statement allegedly made by his parliamentary secretary? I rest my case there, sir.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That this House deplores the government's inability to give leadership in developing and implementing comprehensive and co-ordinated agricultural policies and programs and regrets that by ill-advised and ad hoc remedies the government has weakened the over-all agricultural economy.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in opening this debate I am once again obligated to remind this government that practically every time the subject of agriculture is raised in this House, either in debate or in questions in the House, it is as a result of opposition initiative. It clearly demonstrates our genuine concern for those not only in the industry but for all associated either directly or indirectly with the industry.
There is a host of issues that cry out for attention and there is a host of areas that deserve immediate revision and action.
Agriculture
My colleagues and I will be utilizing the opportunity during the course of this debate to focus government attention on a number of areas of prime concern throughout the country. One such area which has suffered severely, particularly under this administration, is the field of agricultural research and development. This neglect has cost producers, it has cost processors and it has cost consumers alike. Perhaps, and only perhaps, with an impending disaster facing us in the western provinces due to the drought situation will the government finally awaken to the cry for vitally needed research dollars for the purpose of developing and producing drought-resistant crops and drought-resistant grain varieties.
This is the kind of research program that must be given top priority. It is the kind of program that can be developed in field and research stations across the country. The facilities are there, the personnel can be found, but next to nothing has been done and nothing will be accomplished unless adequate funds are made available, and made available immediately. We cannot afford to take the risk of surviving agriculturally in face of a serious and sustained drought. Yet this appears to be a risk that this government is willing to take. This behaviour is totally unacceptable and must be condemned in the harshest terms.
It is time that a federal government which has demonstrated on many occasions its disdain for the health of Canadian agriculture realized the error of its ways. It is my fervent hope that it will not take a complete disaster or total collapse of the industry to bring this about. Obviously, many reforms are needed in the field of agriculture. These should be preceded by experimental trials involving the producer, researcher and processor-the major benefactor being, of course, the consumer. Much greater co-ordination is required at the federal level in terms of organization, with much more of the actual work being carried out at a more regionally based and decentralized level.
One critical problem, as recognized by the Agricultural Institute of Canada, is the constraint on the level of activity of agricultural development and research which is imposed by this government's inability or its unwillingness to pay for it. I can think of no other investment that will provide greater dividends for Canada and Canadians than investment in agricultural research and development. Yet this government remains reluctant to make an adequate commitment and investment.
Declining expenditures on research and development cannot be represented as part of the government's program of restraint initiated in late 1975. The deterioration in research funding really began in 1969 and has continued without pause since that time. It has been accomplished through erosion by inflation. An average National Research Council grant in the biological sciences area in 1974 was 6 per cent larger than in 1969. Its purchasing power was 41 per cent less than in 1969. Salaries and wages have continued to increase, but often after these expenditures are paid no funds remain for actual research work.

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
We are told by qualified sources that as little as 4 per cent of total funds are actually available for research. In terms of the gross national product, Canada spends approximately 1.2 per cent on research and development. This is substantially less than comparable expenditures in France, Germany, Japan, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States, in which countries expenditures range from 1.7 per cent to 2.4 per cent. Current expenditures in Canada are far below the 2.5 per cent which the Senate special committee recommended by 1980.
In this year of the big research budget squeeze most, if not all, are finding the screws particularly tight. For example, Dr. W. E. Tosell, typical of many, and dean of research at the University of Guelph, is trapped in that very squeeze. His budget tells him to trim, and trim heavily, but he says there are no low priority research programs left to cut. Dr. Tosell likens his decisions on research priorities for 1977-78 to the choice that could be forced upon an air traffic controller: Which plane should be allowed to crash, the one with 500 passengers or the one with five? All are important, but obviously you make the decision that will benefit the most people.
This was the rationale that spelled the end to sheep and horse research at the University of Guelph in recent years. This year it spells the end to the mastitis research program. Yet few diseases, if any, continue to cost the Canadian dairy farmer so much in terms of lost production and infected animals being removed from dairy herds. In the past many research programs have been cut. This year both programs and people have to go. This is particularly upsetting in that people cannot be reinstated as easily as programs. When the tap is turned off, that is when people and experience leave. The continuity of programs and overlapping of people during a changeover period is most important information loss.
The situation is so critical in some areas that some of Ontario's marketing boards have been forced to take matters into their own hands. The Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board is taking on an active research role with a $48,000 grant spread over three years. The money is earmarked for sprouting and variety research, two major producer concerns in winter wheat production and marketing. Another example would be the Ontario Pork Producers Marketing Board which is funding a pork research program to the extent of $90,000 this year.
Farmers and farm organizations are clearly worried by the downturn in agricultural research. The need for more federal research funding crops up regularly now during farm conventions and meetings, and so it should. Farmers and the food system combine to produce one out of every three jobs in Canada. Farming had one of the highest productivity increases in the Canadian economy during the past decade, and agricultural exports have been a boon to Canada's trade balance. Putting a freeze on research dollars is self-defeating, and the long-term costs far outweigh the small, short-term savings. The agricultural industry cannot prosper the way it should when an unnecessary freeze is placed on research budgets. The same constraint applies to research and development in general in Canada.
In 1970, the Senate Special Committee on Science Policy reported that Canada's total gross expenditure on research and development had increased from .9 per cent of the gross national product to 1.4 per cent in the period between 1962 and 1967. In 1972 the Senate committee recommended as follows:
National expenditure on research and development should reach 2.5 per cent of the GNP by 1980, it being understood that the Canadian government's direct contribution to reaching this target will be restricted to the support of worthwhile programs and projects.
In the 1980 research and development target of 2.5 per cent of the GNP the Senate committee projected a compound growth rate for the seventies similar to the growth rate for the period 1963-69. Assuming an inflationary factor of only 3 per cent per year, it was estimated that the growth of research expenditures should compound at a rate of 15 per cent annually during the seventies in order to meet the proposed target for 1980. Let us look at what has happened to total expenditures by the Canadian government on research and development since 1967, when the government spent $478.3 million. In 1975 the figure was $861.2 million, representing a growth rate of only 7.63 per cent annually, far short of the 15 per cent proposed by the Senate committee. It has not been sufficient to keep up with inflation during most years, let alone contribute to the advances envisaged by the Senate committee.
In 1972 total expenditures on research and development in Canada had declined to 1.19 per cent of the GNP. This was approximately one-third of the total budget, as opposed to the mid-1960s when the government's contribution equalled one-half of the total expenditure for research and development. Actually, it is the federal government that has led the way in the decline, reducing its support of research and development in Canada from about one-half to less than one-third. The federal government, more than anyone else, has failed to heed the Senate committee's recommendation concerning the financing of research and development and has put an even lower priority on research than it did prior to receiving that committee's report.
Traditionally, the federal government has allocated about one-tenth of its total research and development budget to the Department of Agriculture. Due to the fact that the world situation in agriculture is nearing a crisis point, I suggest it is now time this percentage was increased dramatically. Manpower requirements, present and future, is another area which has been neglected. We are experiencing a shortage of professionals in several disciplines. Policies must be developed at all levels, particularly at the government level, to correct this situation. There is grave danger that the output of trained agricultural scientists will soon be governed by limited Finances instead of by the needs of industry and the country.
The Agricultural Institute of Canada has published five recommendations that would aid the cause of agricultural research. They are: first, unite efforts at all levels for the more effective establishment of priorities in agricultural research and development in Canada; second, develop effective means

May 3, 1977

of ensuring that agricultural research and development programs in Canada are appropriately co-ordinated; third, expand the financial resources available for agricultural research; fourth, regularly determine the professional manpower requirements of Canadian agriculture; fifth, ensure that Canadian educational facilities and resources are adequate for providing the agricultural scientists needed in future.
I am in agreement with these recommendations and urge the government to adopt them. I make the following recommendations: greater emphasis should be placed on research that is done in the field, farms and feedlots across this country, if appropriate, rather than in urban laboratories, and an intensive tackling of other agricultural problems such as the preservation of the small family farm, the development of better and less expensive feed crops and the development and production of drought resistant grasses and grains.
It is interesting to note that when the Agricultural Institute of Canada presented its brief to the Standing Committee on Agriculture on Wednesday, April 27, they summarized their brief with four additional points. I should like to read them into the record. They are as follows:
1.	Canada does not spend enough money on research and development.
2.	Canada does not spend sufficient money on agricultural research and development.
3.	Canada does not spend enough on university based research in agriculture, and
4.	Canada faces an imminent shortage of highly trained manpower to serve biology in the agriculture and food industry.
In conclusion, it reads:
The over-all effects of the above threatens Canada's position as a major world producer and supplier of food. To correct this the government of Canada must reverse the present trend of funding in agriculture and food research and development.
Canada is seriously threatened with the loss of her proud position as one of the world's leaders in the production of food for export. It should be the object of all agricultural organizations and all those concerned about the state of Canadian agriculture to ensure that we maintain an efficient structure for the production, preservation and marketing of food, and that we remain able to share our expertise in the agricultural industry with the developing countries of the world.
One of the fundamental requirements of an efficient food production system is a sound, adequately financed and well co-ordinated research and development capability. This research and development must be directed toward ensuring a continuing supply of food that Canadians can afford, while providing a fair return to the producer and the processor. The food production system should provide a surplus for export which is so very important to Canada's balance of payments in world trade. Among the various faculties of agriculture at several Canadian universities we possess an excellent intellectual resource of scientifically trained academics. It would be constructive to suggest that some aspects of agricultural research be shifted from the city laboratories to the various experimental farms throughout the nation. Many of these regional experimental farms have become almost paralysed simply because of the drastic shortage of funds.
Agriculture
I conclude by asking the federal government to increase its financial commitment to agricultural research. It is to everyone's benefit that our research programs become more intensive. The public, for example, receives the benefit of agricultural research in the form of lower food costs. Funding responsibilities now seem clearly defined. The government foots most of the bill and farm organizations fund special projects. As governments continue to shirk their responsibilities to farmers and consumers alike, more and more farm commodity groups are forced to help support agricultural research. This trend cannot and, indeed, must not continue.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakeroldname: Hon. E. F. Whelan (Minister of Agriculture):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in speaking to this motion I would say that I was surprised, to put it mildly, at its wording and intent. I can only assume that in the motion, facts were disregarded in favour of a purely fictional approach.
The hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) referred to the drought in western Canada. I would like to say a few words on that, if I may. I would like to point out that the hon. member seems to have disregarded the fact that we are a confederation and before the federal government can move in on a program of aid the provinces must request it. We have spent many man-hours working on a program so that it might be ready in case the drought becomes worse. When I say "we" I mean the Department of the Environment, DREE, the Department of Transport, and my own department. All the departments concerned which might be able to participate in this program have asked to pool their resources when the provinces decide what they want us to do. It will then be considered on its merits.
We have been using all the research that is available, and some of the best dry land farming experience and ability is in western Canada at present. These people with knowledge and ability in the field are used all over the world. To hear the hon. member speak, one would think that nothing is known about dry land farming in western Canada. As I said, our researchers and advisers in western Canada on dry land farming are the best in the world. All one has to do is visit some of the areas with this farming problem and one will find that nine times out of ten a Canadian researcher has been there to give advice.
If you visit Mexico and South America you will find there the famous wheat strain called Triticale. It was developed in Manitoba by researchers at the Manitoba university working in conjunction with our researchers. They are all over the world showing people how this special variety of grain was genetically developed. When people from such large countries as the U.S.S.R. and the Republic of China come here, they know where to go. They go to see our research stations and all our people doing agricultural research, because they find it very surprising that a country as far north as ours can be so productive. It is mainly because of the ability of our researchers, plus the ability of our farmers to produce. What amazes them utterly is that all this has been brought about by the

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
close working relationship of our agricultural researchers in CDA working with the provincial departments of agriculture and farmers.
There is no other department in Canada that is more decentralized than Agriculture Canada. This applies mainly to the researchers in our department. They were sent to western Canada before even some of the provinces were created. In some instances they were there even before the settlers arrived, and when the settlers arrived they advised them how to farm. We have done the most superior job in research anywhere in the world.
Certainly, we would like to see more money. I agree with the hon. member that we cannot spend too much money on research. But to say we are doing a poor job is just not correct. For instance, when we talk about cattle, the export of purebred Holstein cattle last year increased by 40 per cent over the previous year. Prices were very good. We export these cattle all over the world. This is done through the Canadian Department of Agriculture, through genetic breeding, research, etc. We have bred some of the best cattle in the world. Our department's researchers have worked with researchers in the provinces. I repeat, we work with the provinces. We have just finished building, in Alberta, a new research station which cost $24 million and houses facilities both for provincial and federal workers at Lethbridge.
Also, in Fredericton, New Brunswick, we have the same kind of station. All the departmental people from the department of agriculture in the province of New Brunswick share the same facilities with the people from the federal department of agriculture. There is no other department that works as closely with the provincial people as we do. I challenge anyone to find another country with a population of 23 million, that is 4,000 miles from sea to sea, and has the agricultural diversification that exists in Canada, that has more people coming from around the world to see what our researchers have accomplished and to learn what will be of help to them and the rest of the world.
I would point out that research is certainly not just a responsibility of the government of Canada. We say that private research is needed and should be encouraged. What is wrong with producers' organizations participating in research programs? I see nothing whatsoever wrong with that. If they want to be part of the over-all program, they have as much right to be there as the government or the private sector.
The development fund for new crop development is now available for research by groups all over Canada. In the area of the hon. member for Elgin, as I am sure he is well aware, there is one of the most advanced research stations on tobacco. People come from all over the world to see what the researchers are doing on new strains of tobacco. Reference was made to this fact by some people who visited me in my office. They called it one of the most outstanding research stations in the world. There is also research on peanuts under the new development fund. It sounds like a "peanut" program, but it is a very important program and we look forward to peanuts being one of our main sources of vegetable oil and also of
[Mr. Whelan.)
protein. It might take the place of some of the other crops that we might not need so badly.
Also, let us consider hybrid corn. In Manitoba they are doing research on hybrid corn. Some hon. members opposite can tell us about the tremendous work they are doing in Manitoba with hybrid corn, where championship yields last year were more than 134 bushels per acre of shelled corn. If it were not for the research that CDA is doing in hybrid corn, we would not be in a position to say that we are producing over 150 million bushels of shelled corn a year in Canada. There are only two other companies doing research in hybrid corn development in Canada besides the government. That is not enough. If it were not for the research we are doing to develop new hybrid strains and use less feed units, it could be grown farther east, north and west than ever before. Corn is one of the most complete grains. It is king of all the grains in the world, and it is exported by the United States more than any other cereal grain.
These are some of the things we are doing here in Canada. We are ready to exchange information on our research with other parts of the world that are in need of it, so that they can properly look after their people. Agricultural research is something we exchange freely with any other nation regardless of political affiliation. We do it for the food of mankind. I am proud of that fact.
The record of this government since I became Minister of Agriculture stands on its merits. Farmers and consumers are benefiting from the development of policies and programs designed to stabilize and ensure producer returns and consumer costs. Net farm income has steadily increased since 1972, when I became Minister of Agriculture. The total for that year was $1.9 billion. That was pushed up to $3.4 billion in 1973- nearly double what it was the previous year. It crept up in
1974	to $3.8 billion. The last figures available show that in
1975	net farm income came to nearly $4.5 billion. Look at the spread-from $1.9 billion to $4.4 billion in three years. Do you call that the result of not supplying leadership and not developing and implementing comprehensive, co-ordinating policies and programs? The facts are simply that agriculture, which was declining in this country in the late 1960s and early 1970s, has experienced a surge of new life. Those facts are solid, and you will find them borne out by the first results of the 1976 census.
How often have we heard people talk about farmers leaving the farm? That has changed, Mr. Speaker. Let me explain. For those who do not know, a census farm is one holding of acre or more, or $1,200 or more in sales. The number of census farms increased by 250 from 1971 to 1976. The growth has been slow, but it is solid. Between 1951 and 1971 the number of census farms had been declining by approximately 13,000 farms per year. That rate of decrease has not only been stopped, it has been stabilized. What is more, the corner has been turned and the figures are beginning to creep up. The area of those census farms increased by a positive 3.4 per cent.
May 3, 1977

We are looking at 166 million acres of farmland which is returning to its farmers enough food to feed the farmer and 52 other people. Twenty years ago the farmer fed himself and ten others. Look at that spread and then tell me honestly that agriculture is a "go nowhere" industry.
Let us look at productivity. Take the man-hour output in 1961, index it at 100, and then see what happens over the next ten years. In the manufacturing sector you see productivity rise to 154.4. In agriculture that increase jumped to 217. It is phenomenal. Farmers are busy people and their work and enterprise added up to mean something like $22.5 billion in retail food sales last year. In terms of actual farm cash receipts, that means a little over 5 per cent of the gross national product or, in dollar terms, about $9.7 billion. And that is just the farmer.
The farmer's business keeps one out of every four Canadians employed. That is how many people work in businesses associated with one stage or another of the food chain. Yet although the farmer provides the key that unlocks the door to prosperity in so many other associated industries, he gets only 38 cents of every dollar that is spent in this country on food. The other 62 cents are split among the food manufacturers, the wholesalers, the distributors, and so on.
Since I have been Minister of Agriculture I have done all I can to make sure that the man on the tractor, the person who milks the cow, or who takes care of the greenhouse, etc., who is responsible for so many other food-associated businesses, knows that he can count on his livelihood. We have seen the National Farm Products Marketing Act come in to give some stability in the marketplace. Under that act we have seen such things as egg prices and supply stabilize. Never mind what you may hear, it is a fact that a dozen grade A, large eggs cost 94 cents in Canada. This morning we checked across the border and the same eggs cost 3 cents per dozen more. The former deputy minister of agriculture has just returned from California, where he said he tried several stores and could not find grade A, large eggs for less than $1.29 per dozen. Last night a man who is with the Dairy Council of Canada told me he had just come back from Burlington, Vermont, where grade A large eggs were $1.11 in the supermarket. So, Mr. Speaker, some of the things that were said about us spending more in Canada are just not factual.
The amendments to the Farm Credit Act have given the young farmer more incentive than ever before to get into and stay in farming. The loan ceiling to farmers under 35 was increased to $150,000. What is more, they were allowed more leeway in terms of time spent off the farm working to support their agricultural ventures. We have seen improvements to the Agricultural Stabilization Act. It has been broadened in scope. Farmers who find themselves in trouble in any particular sector can look for help whether their product falls within the named commodity list or not. To date we have paid out about $55 million to help horticultural producers and beef and dairy cattle farmers.
New tax legislation encourages the maintenance of the family farm. The bill to allow advance payments on storeable
Agriculture
crops is in the other place now. This bill will be a tremendous advance. Every day farmers ask when the other place is going to be Finished with it. I wish they would finish with it, Mr. Speaker. As recently as yesterday Alberta's minister of agriculture was telling farmers to buy more crop insurance. They are extending the program in Alberta to May 6 so they can do that. That program covers "no plant" insurance. If they cannot plant, they are still able to collect some insurance and get paid for part of their operations for the year. That is something a lot of people have not acknowledged. It was used in wet years and now they are going to be able to use it in dry years. I hope they will not have to use it, but it will be available for them. The crop insurance program is being utilized more than ever before with the federal government offering, as an incentive, to pick up 50 per cent of the tab for farmers willing to invest in this sort of protection.
You can say that all this means we are spending more and more money on agriculture. Do you not think the returns justify that kind of expenditures, Mr. Speaker? In comparison with the United States, we are supporting our farmers and the results are showing up in low food costs. I agree that in contrast to the early seventies Canada is now making relatively more payments to its farmers than the United States. I was one of those who continually pointed out that the United States subsidized its farmers more than we did, but that is not true any more. Since that time the United States have seen fit to drastically reduce their commodity support programs while Canada has increased its level of direct payments to producers. Taking the 1975-76 fiscal year, the United States spent $374 on each farmer. Here in Canada the total expenditure per farmer was $1,229. We surpassed them.
It appears that President Carter and the secretary for agriculture may now surpass us, however, with some of the programs they have put before Congress. They recognize what we are doing here as things that would maintain some form of guaranteed income for the farmer and also maintain food production, according to what my officials tell me. This investment is paying off. It is paying off in terms of productivity. It is paying off in terms of agricultural stability and growth. Most of all, it is paying off in helping to keep food costs to the consumer both reasonable and stable. That, of course, is one of the prime objectives of the basic food policy which is in place right now. This government acknowledges the right of consumers to be assured of an abundance of high quality, reasonably priced food. They are getting that food, and they are getting it at rock bottom prices.
The Canadian consumer spends about 18 per cent of his income on food. If he dropped the habit he is developing of taking one meal in every three at a restaurant, the slice of his income would drop, too: it would go down to about 13 per cent; and this is in a society where the trend is more and more to two pay cheque families. But if the consumer is to go on knowing that food will remain available and reasonably priced, then we cannot, as a government, let the Canadian farmer down. Too much depends on him. So he has to be assured of a reasonable return to keep him functioning. With that assur-

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
ance, he will continue to function efficiently. And I am going on record in stating that the Canadian farmer is the most efficient in the world. He is more efficient than the farmer to the south because he has to contend with a much more severe climate and a shorter growing season. He has to house his animals under more severe conditions. He has to use more energy for his poultry and hog production, etc. than farmers in the United States, yet in most cases he can compete with them. That is why I say he is the most efficient farmer in the world.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
The hon. member should consult his mother-in-law, because she has complimented me on what I am trying to do for the farmers. It was the farmer's efficiency that made this country one of the largest donators to the United Nation's World Food Program last year. In 1975 this country was the largest per capita donor of food in the world, with $230 million worth of food going in aid to underdeveloped nations.
Mr. Speaker, some people who delight in making these presentations on behalf of Canada often know nothing about the sweat, toil and tears involved in producing food. The government, however, still wants the Minister of Agriculture to represent us at world food council meetings because they recognize he is the representative of the food producers who make it possible for Canada to be a leader in that kind of program. We are able to give that sort of help because of the way Canada's farmers produce.
Do not think that farmers would work that way if they were not sure that investment of money, time and hard labour was going to pay off. It is paying off, and I am hearing about it. This year at the Canadian Horticultural Council there was a motion passed unanimously and spoken to by representatives from practically every province. They said that this government and this minister had done more for the horticultural industry than any government had in past history. They commended the government for that. The only report I saw of that meeting was carried by the CBC. I spoke at nine o'clock in the morning, and the motion was passed early in the day.
The CBC reporter was the only one covering the motion. It was debated too early in the day for the CP reporters. I guess it was too early in the day for them to be up. So it was only reported by the CBC, or perhaps the other reporters did not want to write the story because it was about something good. As Chief Justice Bora Laskin, and the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) have said, the press does not like to report good news; it reports only the bad news. What is that attitude doing for the unity of the country? If the media
[Mr. Whelan.)
tell our people only the bad things the federal government does, what are the people of the country going to think?
This was a group of people who came from all the areas between Nova Scotia and Vancouver Island. They passed a motion commending the government. However, I have not seen the proceedings reported in any newspaper. I saw a report in a newspaper the other day about the price of food going up. But that report did not talk about the rise in the price of citrus products, about coffee going up over 280 per cent, and about the rise of certain other food costs. The story pointed out-and it is strange to note how newspapers report the rise in food prices-that butter had gone up 10 cents a pound in some cities and 11 cents a pound in others. As well, it was said that "Eugene Whelan, the Minister of Agriculture, said this was a must for dairy farmers." But the story said nothing about citrus fruits grown in the United States or about the citrus pack being 12 per cent larger than it was the year before.
How much are consumers paying for citrus fruit? It is true we have heard many stories of frost damage to that crop. But the question remains, why in heaven's name are we paying more for citrus products? I suggest there is no reason in the world, because the crop is between 10 per cent and 12 per cent bigger than it was the year before. So why should citrus fruit prices be that much higher? Why is someone not asking that kind of question? Of course, there is not much we can do about the price. We import the fruit. We do not grow oranges in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, two years ago we paid the highest price in the world for oranges, for the real McCoy. Why? I suggest the reason is that we do not produce oranges in this country. Therefore, if we fail to produce any product, and import it, we must pay the consequences. We must pay the going rate. We must pay the price the food brokers ask, or go without. Mr. Speaker, if we do not provide security for the producers of our food products, we shall all pay the price. The producers must be able to go to the banks and say, "I want to borrow so many dollars to finance my operations this year." The farmer must be sure of an income with which he can pay off the bank loan. He must have a market for his produce.
If he has no market, if he has no security, what will happen? He will go to the banker who will look at him with his kind eye, his glass eye, and say, "I am sorry; I cannot lend you money because you have no security. There is no guarantee you will pay it back. You have no assured market for your product, and lending you money would be like going to the horse races and betting. Notice, Mr. Speaker, that I spoke of betting at the race track. I did not mention off-track betting.
The horticultural industry has weathered some rough times, but things are now picking up for them. For instance, last year we paid British Columbia horticultural producers more money for their crops than they had received since the stabilization bill was passed. We are now using that act more than ever before. When farmers thank me for some of the things this government has done, I realize they understand our programs and appreciate what we are trying to do for them. As I said, the horticultural industry has weathered some rough times.
May 3, 1977

We are considering the first volume of the Tariff Board report which recommends additional protective measures. Those recommendations will do still more for the horticultural industry.
But things have changed. The picture is not the way it was last year. Farm cash receipts for the fruit and vegetable growers rose to $320 million in 1976, as compared with the $286 million they received in 1975. Those farm cash receipts owed something to the $14.8 million that went from Agriculture Canada, under the stabilization act to growers of carrots, sweet cherries, green plums, summer pears, and so on. We were criticized for assisting the apple growers of Nova Scotia. The Auditor General in his report said we had underestimated our losses. But he did not estimate what we would have spent in unemployment insurance if workers had been laid off, or what the transportation companies and processors and manufacturers would have lost. He did not say what all the people connected with the industry would have lost through unemployment. Luckily, we were able to sell the crop to Great Britain at a reasonable price.
We groan about high food prices in this country, but the facts go against us. In January this year the Ottawa price for sirloin steak was $3.91 per kilo. To the uninitiated let me say that a kilo is a measurement of the metric system. In Washington they were paying $4.01, and in Stockholm over $12. And you think we have high priced butter! Washington is still ahead of us, with a price of $2.91 per kilo. To take Stockholm again, the price there is over $3. In Ottawa, a kilo of butter cost $2.61 in January.
The food price index change-and the latest Figures I could relate to the international picture are for November-shows Canada as the only country among 15 others where the index has dropped about 2 per cent over the year. After us, the United States showed the smallest increase; they were up .7 per cent. In all the talk there is on food, I think it behooves members of this House to remember that food is not a separate subject from agriculture. The one is an extension of the other. The fact that food prices remain reasonable, that farmers continue to produce, and produce effectively, and that agricultural productivity and development in this country is increasing, has a lot to do with the programs and policies instituted by this government.
Let me return for a moment to the subject of research. The hon. member who introduced this motion suggested that we were not employing enough people with Ph.Ds. and high qualifications to do our research. More than ever, graduates of our agricultural schools and universities are returning to the farm. Why are more and more going back to the farm? Because they are going back to the farm, more expertise is available in agriculture. In these days highly educated people are engaged in agriculture. Again I ask, why are they going back to the farm? You know why they are going back. They now have a guarantee that farmers never had before, and those who have been trained in our agricultural colleges and universities may now return to the farm and take advantage of that guarantee. Mr. Speaker, we provide a guarantee for them if
Agriculture
they want to work. We provide nothing for the inefficient farmer. However, if the farmer is productive and efficient, he is going to make a decent living. Let no one say otherwise.
As to ad hockery, I can only say that we have acted in this way when outside forces compelled policy or program modifications. What are we supposed to do if, for example, we are locked into a program so tightly that we cannot move? If world conditions change immediately, what are we supposed to do? Are we supposed to sit and wait? We should be able to act.

speechtext: What about your five-year dairy plan?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: The hon. member mentions the five-year dairy policy. We have deviated from it somewhat, but the present formula is practically the same as before. We have deviated from it somewhat because of world conditions. Mr. Speaker, the former consumer affairs critic of the hon. member's party criticized me for paying dairy farmers too much. Can you imagine a member of the party which proposed this motion criticizing me for paying dairy farmers too much? I got hell for allegedly being responsible for the surplus of their products. Mr. Speaker, Canada depends for its livelihood on productive involvement in the international market. We cannot afford to back ourselves into a corner and act unilaterally. We must keep ourselves flexible and sensitive to outside pressures and changes. We must react to those changes in the interests of our consumers and farmers. I can only suggest, as an example of utter ad hockery, the spirit which moved the motion and brought me to my feet today.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) moved this motion today. As we know, there has recently been a lot of discussion about a food and agriculture policy. In the past we have had many food and agriculture policies. However, we need a much more comprehensive and planned approach toward food and agriculture in Canada. Recently I have been concerned that some of the work done by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs has been dividing farmers and consumers, pitting one against the other. That is the wrong way to start when looking at a food and agriculture policy for this country.
First we had the competition bill that was brought before the House some time ago. It has now had its subject matter referred to one of the standing committees. In that competition bill, according to lawyers for the farm organizations who looked at it, it was found that marketing boards would be rendered illegal, or pretty well useless. In many ways they would become a eunuch, or inoperable for the farmers of this country. The minister said recently outside the House that if that were the case, he would be willing to change the legislation. I hope he makes that commitment to us in a very firm way when that legislation comes before the House if, indeed, he is still Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
Another thing he said is that he has given the Consumers' Association $25,000 to help them understand the bill. That is fine and well. However, he should give some of that money to other organizations such as the Federation of Agriculture so that they can understand the bill as it applies to them. Something else that concerns me in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is that they have come up with a working paper entitled "Competition in Agriculture". The working paper, which I have had a chance to go over very carefully, is in essence an attack on the marketing boards in this country. It recommends a major study of marketing boards with a view toward curtailing their powers because they do not provide enough competition in the marketplace. It does not make farmers efficient or competitive enough.
There are a number of errors in that paper. Some of the more blatant ones are almost ridiculous. One section of the paper refers to fluid milk as a product being under federal supply management. That is not true. It is not a federal supply management commodity at all. When they make errors of that sort, I really wonder about the credibility of their other comments. They go on to talk about the great producer spread in broilers in Canada. Between Vancouver and Toronto there is a spread of three to five cents per pound for producers when they sell their broilers. During the second week of January, 1977, when the spread was three to five cents for producers, the spread at the retail level was 46 cents a pound. In Toronto, broilers were selling for 63 cents a pound, while in Vancouver they were selling for $1.09 per pound-a spread of 46 cents.
The paper dwelt at great length on the immense power of marketing boards, without looking at the other inputs in agriculture that should be examined, such as retailing, processing and input costs to the farmer. Many things in the past have divided the farmer from the consumer. This has been very unfortunate. The Food Prices Review Board did a lot of work. However, too much of the publicity and too many statements by the former chairman of that board-"Ma Plumptre", as some of us called her-were attacks upon farm marketing boards and orderly marketing. They were in ignorance of the other inputs into the cost of food in this country.
In 1969 and 1970 we had the task force on agriculture. It talked about more efficiency in competition in the agricultural sector, and phasing out over half the farmers in this country over the next few years. We had the weakening of the authority of the Canadian Wheat Board through the move of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board in taking the sale of domestic feed grains from under its authority.
We have in this House Bill C-34 which deals with the voluntary pooling of rapeseed, another move which will weaken the authority of orderly marketing in Canada. A short while ago we had the DM-10 report, a document written last summer by senior deputy ministers who were advising the government on food policy. The thrust of that report was toward so-called efficiency, competition and the free market, letting corporations run our food system instead of the producers and consumers collectively.
[Mr. Nystrom.J
We also have the government-and this is where the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) comes in-postponing indefinitely the decision on a national marketing board for broilers. That decision should have been made before now. If the minister checks, he will find that importers of chickens have increased the importation of broilers from other countries by 50 times in the last five years. When you have a supply management and marketing board system such as envisaged here, the quotas in terms of imports from abroad are based on the previous average of your imports. By delaying the decision indefinitely the big importers are able to increase their imports massively and thus destroy one of the intents of orderly marketing. The Minister of Agriculture should make sure his colleague moves much more rapidly than he has in that area.
As I have said before, what we need in this country is an over-all planned and comprehensive approach to a food and agricultural policy. That policy has to cover a whole series of areas. One area we have to look at is farm income. We all know that farm income has been very uncertain, and in many cases inadequate. Farmers not only have the uncertainty of prices here in Canada. Only 50 or 60 percent of their commodities go through marketing boards. They also have the uncertainty of prices abroad. We must consider competition in the world community, weather conditions, world climate conditions, all of which influence the price here at home.
The minister talked about farm income recently going up. However, he stopped with the year 1975. If he had looked at 1976 he would find that net farm income in Canada was down 20.8 per cent from 1975. That is why the minister did not refer to it when boasting about all the things he has done for the farmers. The Outlook conference said that in 1977 it looked as though net farm income would go down by-

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: He could not find the figures.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That is strange. Opposition members can find the figures from the federal department, but the Minister of Agriculture cannot find them. The Outlook conference predicted that in 1977 net farm income would drop by about 40.5 per cent from the 1975 high. There is definitely a downward trend in farming in this country. The minister knows it; we all know it.
Gross cash receipts for the nation as a whole dropped in January, 1977, compared to January, 1976, by 31 per cent, and in western Canada by 38 per cent. It can be seen that farm income is falling. The various programs which the government has in place-some of them good, some going a far distance- are not good enough. They do not provide a secure income for farmers. With that type of fluctuation, it is not secure. What other sector would allow its income to drop by 30 per cent oi 40 per cent over a two-year period? No other sector would allow that.
The second area that we have to look at with regard to a comprehensive food and agriculture policy is that of self-sufficiency, producing vital foods in Canada. We must ensure that we have available in this country a good supply of vital food products. Many people have suggested that by the year
May 3, 1977

2000 Canada will be a net importer of foods, despite the vast acreage, planning and technical skills that we have in our possession. When we import food, we export jobs, not only the jobs of farmers but the jobs of workers in the packaging, handling and processing of food products. Some now say it is a likely circumstance that we will become a net importer of food. Federal government figures show that without the export of grain and oil seeds Canada would already be faced with an agricultural deficit of some $1.5 billion. For a country of this size, that is an utter disgrace. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture cannot be proud of that fact.
Also, we have all kinds of tariff inequities. We have a great deal of protection for some of the manufacturing in Central Canada. We have a great deal of protection for a lot of manufacturing in the minister's own area of southern Ontario. But when it comes to the farmers, do you know what the average protection is? It is about one half of 1 per cent. In summary, then, we have to be self-sufficient in basic foods in order not to just look after ourselves and keep farmers on the land and provide more jobs for Canadians in the future, but also to protect our consumers against very high prices over which they will have no control unless we produce these foods ourselves.
The minister talked about oranges coming in from abroad, saying we had no control over these prices. If we do not become self-sufficient in a lot more foods, if we continue to let our self-sufficiency erode, there will be many more products over the price of which we will have no control when we buy them in the supermarkets in a few years, time.
Another area which greatly concerns me is that of the quality and safety of food in this country. People would benefit from a system which emphasized nutrition as one of our highesi priorities. If this were made a primary goal of the national food policy, you would first of all have decreased health costs. Surely, preventive medicine is the best part of medicine. Surely, it is desirable to bring down the cost of health services in this country. One of the best ways of doing this is through better nutritional programs. The Food Prices Review Board said two years ago, in one of its good reports, that about 40 per cent of the hospital days in Canada may be indirectly linked with the type of diet we follow-to the types of food consumed by Canadians. A report from the United States says that about six of the leading ten causes of death in that country may be linked to the type of food people there are eating.
We could have decreased health costs. We could have increased productivity by Canadians if our people were healthier, and we could have a much better quality of life if we had nutritional programs. So far, such programs have been a dismal failure. They have been disgusting. We have junk food in most of the schools in this land. We see the increased consumption of pop, chips and foods of that sort. In the United States, in the Second World War, the consumption of pop went up by 85 per cent. In some states kids are now consuming
Agriculture
three bottles of pop a day. The consumption of milk has gone down. We should have a school milk program. Governments, both federal and provincial-we can all share in the responsibility-spend very little on promoting nutrition in Canada.
The blame falls on all parties equally. All governments have spent, in the last year, less than $1 million on promoting nutritional goals in Canada. The food industry, by comparison, spent in the last year over $90 million promoting food, and much of the food they promoted is of questionable nutritional value. All one has to do is to sit down with a small child and watch television and see what kind of advertising gets through to the small child. It isn't advertising of wholesome and natural foods; it is advertising food of very little, or negative nutritional value.
We have in our food system about 1,800 different chemicals and additives. Most of them are not there to improve nutrition or to improve food in terms of the income of farmers. Most of them are there for convenience or to make it look sexier, or the skins look redder, or they are there for the sake of the profits of large corporations in the food industry. So we need changes to improve the quality and safety of our food in terms of the health of our nation.
The fourth area about which I am very concerned-the honourable member for Elgin has already spoken at length about this-is that of research. I concur in what he said. There ought to be more research, particularly in the university community, research which will help find some of the nutritional answers which are so badly needed by Canada as a nation, research which will help the farmer improve his commodities and improve his life style and income, research which will perhaps solve some of the problems which we will be facing shortly as energy prices increase, as the energy input into the whole food sector is probably the most intensive, in terms of agriculture, in North America. These are areas in which we need to move. Too much of the research done by the private sector today is with one goal in mind-the enhancement of profits, of greater convenience in selling certain commodities, square tomatoes, four-legged chickens, or what-have-you. That is the type of research which is done throughout Canada.
The fifth area which it is important to consider in terms of a new food and agriculture policy is that of resources. First of all, we have the question of land use. The Department of Agriculture has stated that about 250 acres of good quality farmland goes out of production every day. That is more than 10 acres an hour-land we cannot recover. The Agrologists Institute of Canada stated recently that we have in this country some 44 million hectares of land which we can farm. That represents only 4.87 per cent of our total land mass. Of that, only 7.3 hectares, or .8 per cent of Canada's land mass, is good quality land in areas where there is a reasonable climate. If we continue present policies, by the year 2001, according to the agrologists, about one-third of our good quality land will be under concrete and beyond retrieval by future generations. So we have to look at resources; we have to look at the

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
question of energy; we have to look at the question of allocating energy in a much more rational way.
The last area we should consider in terms of food policy is market power itself. We have to do something to control the processors and the retailers. We have the Mallen report which states we are paying about 4 per cent more than we should because of the lack of competition in the food system in Canada. A series of recommendations is made. We had the Barber commission which also made a series of recommendations with respect to the cost of farm machinery. All kinds of studies have brought to our attention a number of things which should be done.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, we need, in a food policy, provision for orderly marketing. The farmer has to have some security. He has to have some clout in the marketplace when he markets his commodities. I should like to move an amendment and perhaps speak to it for a few moments thereafter.
I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That the motion be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma and adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and this House further regrets the government's failure to give full support to an orderly marketing system which would give producers the collective strength to reduce corporate power in the food system and stabilize farm incomes as well as prices to consumers.''
I move that motion because I think a major part of food and agriculture policy in Canada has to be an orderly marketing system under which the farmer has stability of income and the consumer, on the other hand, has stable prices. We have too many of our foods on the open market system where the farmer does not know from one day to the next what he is going to get for the food he produces, while the consumer, on the other hand, does not know what he will have to pay for the food he is going to have to buy.
It is important that this House should say to the government: We have not gone far enough in the direction of orderly marketing. There have been too many attacks on the orderly marketing system. We only have in Canada three national supply management programs. There are about 100 different marketing boards, most of them under provincial jurisdiction. I think it is important that at this time, when the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is attacking the orderly marketing system, this House should say to the government that we should have more orderly marketing in Canada for the sake of both farmers and consumers.
It is very strange that some people are saying that the three orderly marketing systems we have are very bad-that they are really bad in terms of producing food because they are supply management programs. But almost every other industry in Canada practices supply management. If you follow the same philosophy vis-a-vis the unemployed, since we have an oversupply of workers you reduce wages in this country. Of course, we would not stand for that, and rightfully so. But when farmers are faced with oversupply the price that they get for their product is reduced.

There is now also oversupply of farm machinery. If we did not have supply management, the price of combines and tractors should be dropping until that supply is used up. But that is not happening. If doctors or lawyers were being paid too much, they would argue that we should be bringing in cheaper lawyers and doctors from England or overseas; they would work for less and undercut the Canadian supply. But we do not do that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to begin by saying that opposition days, especially those devoted to Canadian agriculture, come so seldom in this House that it is always a little difficult to know just where to start; there is so much to be said about so many different facets of Canadian agriculture by so
May 3, 1977

many in this House, especially those in the official opposition. I wish to confine my remarks to just two aspects of this opposition day debate, and they are very closely related. They are the western drought situation, which is very serious indeed in western Canada, and the total Canadian beef cattle industry as at this time of year, the end of the first quarter of 1977.
Two weeks ago today I spoke in the budget debate on this same theme, with appropriate comments and recommendations pertaining to budget considerations. Today I wish to update those earlier comments. In that two-week interval the drought situation has worsened over the entire western Canadian front. It extends from the interior of British Columbia right across the prairies to the east side of the province of Manitoba. It is part and parcel of a much bigger drought area in the United States covering the southwestern states, including west Texas, some of the midwestern states, the northwestern states bordering on Canada, and the Pacific coastal states of California, Oregon and Washington.
We are hearing more and more of the inevitable comparisons between the ten years of the dirty thirties and the present crisis. I was personally involved in those earlier difficult days. Southeastern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan had the doubtful distinction of being the drought capitals of Canada, especially my home city of Medicine Hat. The comparisons that we are making today are very valid. The public at large, even in western Canada, is not aware how serious the situation really is. Even younger farmers do not fully appreciate the present situation, and certainly not the serious consequences which will continue to escalate as the drought persists for two years, five years-who knows, maybe another ten years.
Hon. members should have noticed the picture which appeared on page 8 of today's Globe and Mail showing a wide section of harrows almost covered over with drifted soil. The picture was taken in the Regina area. This picture could have been resurrected from 40 years ago, except that it showed a very wide harrow set-up not generally used in the thirties. Yesterday's Ottawa Journal carried this brief item under the column, "Canada in brief'. The heading read, "Dust storm eases", and was datelined Regina. It read:
A severe 12-hour dust storm has swept down on this city after the dryest prairie winter in 100 years tapered off Sunday, leaving a faint pall of dust still hanging on the horizon. Winds of 50 mph tore across southern Saskatchewan Saturday, stirring up the worst dust storm so far this spring in the usually windy and dry provincial capital. The prairies are dryer than they have been for almost 100 years.
Also in yesterday's Globe and Mail there was a front page story about the California drought, and in the county of Marin the initials BYOB mean "Bring your own bottle". Of water, of course, not booze. Yesterday's Calgary Albertan had the front page headline, "Water crisis closer", and the aritcle went on to describe the town of Crossfield, 30 miles north of Calgary, where the town's water supply could dry up within ten days. There is also an emergency domestic water crisis at Olds, Alberta, north of Calgary, which is not usually considered in the drought area. At Didsbury, Alberta, there is another water crisis. There is even an indication in the Albertan story that the city of Calgary may perhaps have a water shortage, which
Agriculture
is related to five years of less than normal precipitation; and there is a plea to Calgary residents to conserve water.
In my own city of Medicine Hat the South Saskatchewan River is at least as low as it was during the thirties. But there is this difference, Mr. Speaker. Today the exposed shorelines are visibly green with algae pollution caused by upstream sewage effluent, and this is causing extreme concern and difficulties in water treatment and pumping for irrigation use.
To understand the background of this drought picture we must appreciate that even though last year's grain crops were above average, to all the way to excellent, western Canada has experienced three winter droughts, the most severe being the last winter from which we have just emerged. Snowfall was much below normal, and snow moisture which was available, was eventually lost by evaporation due to our Chinook winds. These chinook winds blow year round. We usually bless them in the winter and curse them in the summer, since they do cause loss by evaporation of about 40 inches of precipitation a year, and that is of water, not snow. That is four times our average snow and rain precipitation. Over most of the western prairies there has been no rain of any consequence since last August. In the extreme southern parts of Alberta and Saskatchewan adjacent to the United States border there has been no rain of consequence since last June.
Members will appreciate the special significance of the drought in western Canada if they are reminded that out of a total of 50 million acres of usable grasslands for domestic livestock, mostly cattle in all of Canada, some 45 million acres are in the prairie provinces. Most of this acreage is well within the present drought area. Some 150 years ago these same western plains, consisting of approximately 130 million acres, because there were no cultivated lands then, supported six million buffalo, six million antelope, a million mule deer, and a million elk. Today, the 45 million acres of western grasslands carry about six million cows. That is about twice as many cows as there were during the thirties.
Range management authorities believe these serious drought cycles have been part of our North American weather and climate patterns for many centuries and they will continue to be part of our present and future weather cycles. Some authorities suggest that our short grass plains areas of western Canada were the result of excess summer grazing by the buffalo, especially during drought cycles. Whatever the reasons or circumstances associated with these serious drought cycles, the important thing that we learned, or should have learned, from the experiences of the thirties respecting our grasslands is that our cattle numbers must be adjusted downward to fit the reduced carrying capacities of our ranges.
I seriously question the wisdom of feeding expensive feed, either hay or supplements, on bare ground for prolonged periods at this time of year. This is what is happening in parts of western Canada right now. Some of it is recommended by provincial governments. That same feed will be needed next winter for our cow herds. There was a reasonable carryover of
5246

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
hay after our very mild winter, but it naturally follows that the prospects for the new hay crop almost nil.
Last week the press carried various news stories about the indication of a drought assistance program announced by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). I was out there most of last week. The press carried a report on three different aspects: there would be assistance for deep well development; pumping of water to fill stock water reservoirs, dams and dugouts; and assistance to move cattle, presumbably to a new source of grass or feed. No other details were provided: at least, I did not read or hear them. I trust more details will follow shortly on the total program.
The urgency should be apparent to all. The first two items on deep wells and long distance water pumping are most commendable. I will make a further comment later on these two points. However, with respect to the item relating to the federal government's assistance to move cattle out of the drought areas, surely this suggestion begs the question: Where could they be moved to? The grassland drought area is so vast that there is no available pasture in western Canada. Cattlemen have been moving their cattle in large numbers for over two months now, either directly into feed lots in western Canada for finishing, or through the market system to Ontario for spring and summer grazing and finishing next winter.
In a survey conducted by my office covering 19 cattle market outlets across southern Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, I have estimated the volume of this drought cattle movement is up by almost 50 per cent over previous years. The only grass in western Canada that just might be available, with federal action, is some of the 1,000 square miles within the Suffield National Defence reserve.
On April 19 the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard), responsible for the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, indicated in committee that the Suffield PFRA pasture would be opened this year. Surely this decision could be forthcoming immediately and, hopefully, for an enlarged area available for grazing. If it is not asking too much, I would like to request that the forgotten domestic animal, sheep, be given a place on the Suffield lands in the form of a special community pasture exclusively for sheep.
I have given the House a background review of the western drought, as I see it, and as one who was very much involved and influenced by the prolonged drought in the thirties. It is only natural that I should have some personal recommendations for a federal government emergency drought program. I would like to indicate a few points on that program at this time. First, and most important, we should recognize that there is a genuine and urgent need for the mutual co-operation of cattle producers, the federal government and the provincial governments on the prairies.
Cattlemen are already reducing their cattle numbers drastically. In so doing, they will be faced with abnormally high income figures for 1977 and later years if the drought persists and becomes worse. I suggest the federal government's tax policy should permit some form of income to be set aside for these emergency cattle sales-that is, the income from them-

on a tax free basis provided they are reinvested into cattle purchases. This is not just before the end of the following year but at the end of this present drought cycle.
In addition, provision must be made for cattle producers who allow their herds to increase after the drought, by natural increments, to be eligible for this special tax incentive. This is necessary, since an adequate grass cover could take several years to develop after the drought ends. Provincial governments already have the means to make their contributions by the use of their lease rental formulas for determining grazing rents. Carrying capacities will be much lower, so lease rentals should reflect this lower carrying charge. We should note that a somewhat similar tax incentive program for cattle has already been initiated in the United States.
The crash program for deep wells and long distance water pumping should be given to the technical arm of the federal government, which I think is ideally suited for this. I am referring to the PFRA. This agency has the experience and the know-how, so let us turn them loose, with instructions to act immediately. I can only assume that such a crash program would also be available to small towns with a domestic water shortage. Is it not appropriate now to support the suggestions of other members of this House that PFRA be returned home to the Department of Agriculture, where it belongs? The same climatic conditions exist today that gave birth to PFRA in the mid-thirties under the department of agriculture. If a sense of rededication for the survival of the prairies is needed by PFRA and by the government, surely that need is here now, with this drought.
It is my understanding that some behind the scenes meetings have been going on with various government agencies and the western provinces. If there is co-operation here, let us hear about it in regular information releases. Is there some joint action, if only to share information with the United States, on this whole question of drought? I am sure that country will willingly share its resource knowledge on this subject with Canada. There are indications that the drought is more critical in the United States. Authorities at Iowa State University at Ames, Iowa, have taken a special interest in this subject and have indicated that last summer the drought centre for North America was about over Sioux Falls, South Dakota, and that this centre is now moving northwesterly right for our Canadian prairies. Most of us in the west would agree, and quickly add, that it has already arrived there. We must also note that the U.S. Congress has passed legislation to aid drought-stricken areas in 17 western states, and the United States department of interior will provide interest-free loans to farmers and others forced to buy water because of the drought.
I want now to make some specific comments about our Canadian cattle industry and, more particularly, about federal government policies dealing specifically with cattle. During the Christmas recess, when the House was not in session, three very important policy announcements were made. At no time was there an adequate opportunity to debate these cattle
May 3, 1977

policies, even after the House resumed the winter session. I say very sincerely that this is most regrettable. The three policy announcements were: first, on December 23, 1976, the beef import policy for 1977 by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce and the Department of Agriculture; on January 4 of this year, the cow-calf program for 1977; and on January 24 of this year the fed cattle support program for 1976.
On the first one-that is, the 1977 policy for beef imports- I spoke in some detail two weeks ago during the budget debate. It is noteworthy that last Sunday on CBC's "The Nation's Business" the minister made reference to this policy and suggested it had been requested by cattle producers. He might have been a little more specific. Cattlemen were asking for this action to control imports a year earlier than mid-October, 1976, when the government first introduced beef controls, the day after the U.S. triggered their meat import law.
I will only add to my earlier remarks on this policy that the government's lack of response by suitable action in the spring of 1976, after which a 60 per cent increase in offshore beef occurred for the calendar year 1976, that this deliberate political action delayed the long overdue recovery in the cattle and beef marketplace by a full year. Even today, in spite of the 1977 beef import agreements-and they are not official trade treaties, but only another form of a gentlemen's agreement which gave us so much trouble last year-there are clear indications that offshore 1977 beef imports from Australia are now up by over 90 per cent over 1976 for the first 3'/2 months of this year.
