speechtext:
I appreciate your comments, Mr. Speaker, and I will try to complete my remarks quickly. As I was saying, there were clear indications that offshore 1977 beef imports from Australia are now up by over 90 per cent, that is, in the first Vh months of this year. Surely we will not see a repeat of last year and see the present upturn in cattle markets, which is occurring right now, choked off for a second time by political action. That could well lead to the final demise of our cattle industry.
The second announcement was the January 4 cow-calf stabilization policy. It was a long overdue policy statement and was received pretty well by our cow-calf producers. It follows the minister's own stabilization legislation. However, after all the troubles of the cow-calf producers throughout 1976-and I happen to think it was the worst year ever for cow-calf producers-and after the personal promises of the minister to
Agriculture
cattle producers and to provincial ministers of agriculture, we find that this policy covers only 1977 and is not retroactive to 1976, when surely it was most needed. I repeat, this was after the minister had promised a cow-calf policy for 1976 in 1976. Why not? I can only suggest that the reason can be lack of support in cabinet for the minister's recommendations.
The third and last policy announcement the day before the House resumed sitting announced the government's fed cattle support price for 1976 and the resulting payouts for three of the four quarters last year. I want to point out that the payout-and it was welcomed by some pretty desperate cattle producers-would never have been necessary had those offshore beef imports been properly dealt with and had they been held to historical levels throughout 1976. In arriving at this support level the minister had to change his own rules. First, he used 95 per cent instead of 90 per cent as the factor to adjust the previous five-year average, and then he used the flat dollar figure-$1.69 or something like that-to compensate for the cost of production factor. During 1976 it was generally agreed that the two principal input costs, that is, feeder cattle and feed-barley in the west, and corn in the east-were lower than the previous year. This should have lowered the support price. The minister has never explained how he arrived at this payout plan.
I should like to conclude these remarks about our cattle industry by urging the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald), the Minister of Agriculture, and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien), all of whom are involved in the future of our cattle production, to think long and carefully about the political direction that Canada's cattle industry should take. I sincerely hope that they will give consideration to letting our price system function and letting the consumer pay for the groceries, including beef, at the checkout counter rather than at tax time. Let us keep freight rates neutral among commodities, and let us concentrate on the economic management of the whole economy in order to stay competitive with our international trading partners and hold input costs down to a reasonable level. Canada's cattle industry is at a crossroad, the most critical one in our history. I have no doubt it will survive, if only because of those 45 million acres of native grasslands in western Canada that by and large will continue to be grazed by cattle, but surely our survival must depend on a truly market oriented basis.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is once again being asked for more money, but nobody seems to worry about where it will get it or think about the vehemently denounced $7 billion deficit which was mentioned a few days ago.
Mr. Speaker, I, for one, advise my hon. friends to abide by the following golden rule: If you want to get happier-or less unhappy, as the case may be-keep clear of governments, whether they are red, blue or grey. Farmers apparently have earned themselves the reputation of being constant complain-
80012-531/2

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
ers. Some of them probably are, for governments have caused them to become so dependent that every year, time and again, agriculture in Canada is in a state of crisis. I am working and shall continue to work towards making them as free as possible. If the situation remains the same, however, producers should not be held responsible. On the other hand, if the necessary adjustments are made, the government should not yield to blackmail, no matter where it is coming from. Adequate information will be necessary. One thing is certain, and it is that farm producers have become businessmen, and they will have to behave as such, something for which they are quite ready.
As for the government, it has the responsibility of ensuring the support required to confirm Canadian agriculture in its proper rank, in its industrial structure, while ensuring a transition to protect the agricultural producers who cannot attain the level of a profitable undertaking, perfectly integrated in the overall Canadian agriculture. Still, all the advantages of the industrialist cannot be had without paying the cost of the inconveniences: it will be one or the other, the individual will have to make a choice and assume its consequences.
Today's motion is an ideal occasion to reflect on the role each one must play, here and elsewhere; first of all in the House, where the opposition will be either enlightened and dynamic or negative, destructive, more or else opportunist, even clumsy. To the government, it gives the opportunity to explain specific points; to national associations and organizations, to express themselves in national terms; to unions, to ponder their own responsibilities, because there is no field other than agriculture in which unions and government work so much together. Finally, it gives producers themselves the opportunity to consider what they can expect and must give, what they can receive and the cost they must pay.
For instance, to accuse the government and implicate the House in deploring the fact that the government is incapable of setting up a policy, complete and coordinated programs, to profess that the House regrets the fact that the government has weakened rural economy through inconsiderate expedients, says everything and nothing. If governing is the art of making choices, I feel the opposition then has no talent for governing. It is also bungling the opportunity of discussing agriculture, efficiently and responsibly, while being practical and realistic. It is also a waste of time, as such accusations can have no repercussions in the real needs of producers. It is also and finally to prove an almost total lack of consultations between the opposition and farmers' groups, set up by them and for them. In short, this is the question the opposition should ask: Is everything still to be done in the field of agriculture or has the government failed in what it has done? Let us agree on one point: if the government were to do more, it should increase the farm income, reduce the farmer's week, provide him with all sorts of guarantees and solve all his problems, in short, it would be paradise on earth.
In answer to the opposition's questions, I would insist on two points: first, the 1977-78 dairy policy and, second, agriculture and alimentation as experienced by Agriculture Canada and

by the government. This policy, Mr. Speaker, is the tangible recognition of an equity principle between the natural milk and the industrial milk sectors. Indeed, an injustice existed between natural milk and industrial milk producers. The government, through its policy, solved the problem of cumbersome surpluses which were accumulated by the producers themselves, but almost without their knowledge. This was done with the tacit endorsement of certain leaders who put the interests of industry-if not their own-before those of a great many primary producers, particularly small ones.
The 1977-78 dairy policy enabled the government to pay an accrued debt of $152 million in order to refrain from having to mortgage unduly the future and to jeopardize rural economy. The dairy policy has also been the consecration of a $2.66 subsidy on the occasion of its implementation which, as hon. members know, should be gradually reduced. Third, the policy also was an opportunity to demonstrate that indexing could be made to work, even if it was to be passed on to the consumer. This way we could see the price of butter increase from $1.08 to $1.18 and the price of milk powder from 68 cents to 70 cents. The dairy policy was also an opportunity to see the milk quota raised to $105.6 million a hundredweight.
Industrial milk producers also had a guarantee, namely that the maximum deduction would never exceed $125 million in the future. Furthermore, the dairy policy made it possible to reduce the deduction to $1.20 while it should have amounted to $1.91 if policy data had been applied mechanically. The 1977-78 dairy policy allowed for a real increase in the producer's revenue. The net revenue of $10.10 in 1976-77 is increased to $10.66 in 1977-78, the highest level ever reached; it was $10.57 in 1975. However, we can remember that at that time there was still a milk war and that there were some rumours about a war over production costs.
This 1977 dairy policy forced the government to invest some $477 million which were distributed as follows: $266 million in subsidies, $20 million in marketing costs, $15 million in export costs, $20 million in the form of world food assistance, $4 million for market analysis, sales promotion and research and finally $152 million which represent the debt remittance from the transfer payments fund. Here are as many positive advantages which are exactly the contrary of the ill-advised and ad hoc remedies mentioned in the motion which was put forward today by the opposition. Of course, the average contribution of 25 cents a hundredweight of milk provided for the fluid milk supplies which should help pay part of the export costs for milk products made quite a few hon. members jump.
It is quite true that one's man joy is another man's sorrow but we should consider that this 25 cents is an acknowledged principle of interdependence between industrial milk producers which indeed has an impact on their current and future incomes. That point has to be understood, Mr. Speaker, and has to be made understood.
In addition, this milk policy is also the sanction of an equity principle, that is the end of an inequity which has existed
May 3, 1977

because of the manipulation performed by some leaders in the Canadian milk industry. All they want now is to save face and, to do so, they keep on misleading producers. That is why today I take the liberty of putting a formal request before the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) so he might offer evidence of this interdependence and equity established through the 1977-78 policy. The minister must also publish the quotas of all Canadian producers from 1974 to now and keep on doing it in the future.
Finally, if necessary the Canadian Dairy Commission must recuperate the administration and the distribution of quotas but, for the time being, it must provide for a fair distribution. The government acted in the interest of the dairy industry, and even though the conflicts of interest and the tactics of some dairy leaders allude to the contrary, future and truth will prove that the minister and the government were right. That is another glaring evidence that the government made the right move.
In a much more general viewpoint, that of food, the government did achieve what I shall call a real performance. Obviously, it is not a matter of food for angels, nor is it paradise on earth, but this is a matter of food in general, which passes through the producer, the processor, the wholesaler, the retailer and the consumer.
Agriculture overlaps the food circuit together with the processing and distributing sectors, in order to meet one of the most basic needs of people. That circuit implies two characteristics that seem not to be as obvious in other economic sectors: It is very fragmented and gets into a most important part of our economy. This diversification makes the participation of the government absolutely necessary, particularly in the fields of research and regulation. There are more than 300,000 primary producers and, as it is obviously impossible for an individual farmer to do large-scale research, the Minister of Agriculture takes this responsibility and the government finances research projects such as those carried out in educational establishments like Saint-Hyacinthe college or Laval University.
Another result of the diversification of the agricultural sector is the fact that farmers are unable to have a real influence on a market subject to cyclical variations. Since agricultural markets tend to extend beyond regional and even national boundaries, their regulation must be carried on by the government. The second characteristic of our food chain is its numerous ramifications. The basic Canadian economic activity is, directly or indirectly, largely dependent upon farming and food industry. Agricultural products account for 18 per cent of total Canadian freight and about 25 per cent of the total volume of goods carried through the St. Lawrence Seaway. In addition, about 3 per cent of the volume of fuel and lubricants sold in Canada are used by various farming vehicles. The handling of agricultural products and supplies gives work to 25 per cent of the Canadian wholesale trade labour force.
Besides, food industries and manufacturing of a large variety of farm material and supplies are sectors of primary importance. Our society and our economic system are becoming ever
Agriculture
more complex. For example, pesticides which were seen without any reservation as blessings a generation ago now require severe control. That is one of the very many areas where, within the framework of the government's global objectives, the Department of Agriculture has to play a more important role.
The department determines well the problems which concern Canadians, and it does so with limited resources as we know. Indeed, the part of the budget and the staff allocated to the Department of Agriculture during those few last years do not reflect its increasing importance. In fact, 2.2 per cent of government expenses are allocated to agriculture, while the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce administers no less that one fourth of them. To respect government priorities and meet public needs they reflect, the Department of Agriculture has evolved towards greater decentralization. Our expenditures vary from province to province in direct proportion to their farming operations. It goes without saying that our research stations must go in climatic and pedagogic areas suited to their research objectives. For example, the results obtained at the Ste. Foy Experimental Farm might not be useful in the Peace River area, so there is a research station in Alberta. The physical distribution of our experimental farms and other regional offices is but one aspect of the close relationships we maintain with the agrifood sector.
The Department of Agriculture of Canada is actively co-operating with many other departments. In addition, in view of the distribution of powers between the federal and provincial governments with respect to agriculture, a close relationship is maintained with provincial departments and deputy ministers of agriculture. The Canadian Farm Services Co-ordination Committee and its sub-committees, as well as the Canadian Agriculture Research Council are good examples of ongoing co-ordination mechanisms linking both levels of government, those representing the sector, colleges and universities. Those co-ordination committees are interested in various aspects of agriculture varying from grain diseases to the management of farm operations. Some of them study the basic principles and resources of agriculture, namely climate and land fertility.
Mr. Speaker, I could continue but I will conclude by summarizing very briefly the challenges that the present Minister of Agriculture decided to take up with the government. Second, the government protected agriculture from a multitude of natural calamities. Third, the government protected the farming sector from temporary market disruptions, and the milk policy is a clear proof of that. The government also improved and broadened its farm markets. The government also helped improve the structure of the agrifood sector. The assistance to developing countries is another illustration of departmental concerns. Of course, a lot remains to be done, and this government is there and helping effectively in terms of producers' needs, and I hope as you do for an ever more adequate answer in that direction.

May 3, 1977
Agriculture

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the motion introduced by the Conservative party, which reads as follows:
That this House deplores the government's inability to give leadership in developing and implementing comprehensive and co-ordinated agricultural policies and programs and regrets that by ill-advised and ad hoc remedies the government has weakened the overall agricultural economy.
Mr. Speaker, this motion gives us the opportunity to discuss once more a vital problem in Canada, that of agriculture. First, I wish to commend the hon. member who proposed the motion on the agricultural policy. I think that after the agricultural disaster of the last twelve months, it is important for every member of the House of Commons to study the situation in order to prevent its recurrence. For several years, I have realized that too often in agriculture we have a policy of expediency and short-sighted programs. Sometimes, we appeal to grain producers, sometimes to beef, hog, chicken producers when it is not to dairy producers urging them to increase their production. This government even offered bonuses to those who would produce more. But a few months later, it offered bonuses to destroy that production and only twelve or thirteen months ago, the minister had to face a production surplus that could not be sold.
The studies were not comprehensive enough, the markets were considered only on 12- or 24-month periods and the victim of that lack of foresight was the agricultural producer. Not only the farmer must face alone the whims of the weather, but he must cope with the fluctuations of domestic and foreign markets. He cannot get the protection needed against excessive imports, if not against dumping. The only answer proposed by this government is the following: decrease or simply discontinue production.
We have witnessed that shameful attitude of a government which should support the efforts of producers in the wheat issue, when several million tons of wheat have been left rotting in the fields, or when the producer was given a subsidy not to sow his land while millions of human beings were starving. All farmers will remember the call of the Minister of Agriculture in favour of beef production. An unbelievable number of dairy producers abandoned milk production and turned to that promising business only to realize a few months later that they had been taken in. They produced at lost because the feed grain prices had increased twofold. That was a failure for most eastern producers who had to rely on imports of western grain.
We have noted the same failure in egg and broiler chicken production, when uncontrolled imports obliged producers to run at only 50 per cent of their capacity. Now what about milk producers and dairy products? I think all farmers will long remember the year 1976-77 when some of them had to pay $5,000 and even $6,000 as a penalty for overproduction.
Mr. Speaker, I am ashamed to talk of over-production. Could we ever have imagined that, in 1976, we would have forced our farmers to throw away their milk if they did not want to be fined? Yet, this is what happened. It is enough to make you think that a somewhat responsible government

cannot make forecasts for two or three years, when normally its policy should cover at least five years. As a result of this lack of foresight, in 1977 we have only 46,000 dairy farms left from the 96,000 we had in 1970.
We still import more than 60 million pounds of cheese and millions of pounds of butter, and the authorities say that this is normal; in fact, it is very difficult to learn the exact quantity. We import more than 80 kinds of cheese. And I note on the list of imported cheese some types, like Cheddar, which have priority in Quebec and of which we produce an excellent quality. Why must we look elsewhere? The same thing could be said about butter.
During my visit to British Columbia, I asked a distributor why he had only imported butter in his storage facilities. He told me that it was the only type available. That brought to my mind the warehouses in Quebec that are quite full and cannot find buyers. We should put an end to these ridiculous situations. This year the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) wanted to give new hope to our dairy producers, who did not seem to be able to regain their position after last year's disaster. Because of the $8.60 a hundredweight fine on overproduction which was needed to bring about an average reduction of 18 per cent of the dairy production in 1976-77, the producers had to sell part of their herd or to stop milking their cows in the last months of the year so as not to be ruined by the fines.
This is how production in 1976-77 was limited to 9.7 billion pounds. This year, the revenue level wished for 1977-78 is $11.86 a hundredweight with 3.5 per cent butter-fat, for a federal grant of $2.66 a hundredweight. This increase of 41 cents over last year is not even equivalent to the cost of living indexation of 9 per cent recommended by the Anti-Inflation Board. It is not, as has been said, based on the increase in the production costs either, since the input cost increase is well over 41 cents. We must also consider the processor, to whom the minister suggests that-he pay the producers $9.20 a hundredweight on reception.
Does the minister realize that processors will find it hard to meet his request, because they also have to face increases in wages and all other operating costs. The figures mentioned by the minister in his statement for costs to be incurred afterwards are rather provisional or fictitious, because there are too many contingencies. The same goes for the $152 million the minister undertook to write off. Those $152 million cover only the amount paid by producers who delivered surpluses, for which they payed penalties. But what about all those who were forced to sell part of their dairy cattle, if not all of it, at rock bottom prices to pay their debts? What about the others who produced milk all through winter and had to discontinue milking their cows? Those farmers will not recoup their losses before one or two years.
Let us come back to the matter of quotas. Last year, all producers had their quotas reduced by 20 per cent. It would be only reasonable that after the increase in national quota volume, those producers got free the 20 per cent taken away from them. This is not what is currently done, because pro-
May 3, 1977

ducers must pay to get back the volume lost on their former quotas. I hope the minister will establish a specific program so every producer receives fair treatment from regional agencies.
The minister delegated to dairy producer unions the reponsi-bility for administering quotas for the government. He deserves commendation for having directly involved farmers through their unions. There will be a benefit, in that producers complaining about their quotas will not have to come to Ottawa any more to register their protests with the minister. They will simply force their leaders to do their duties. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) announced a $200 million increase relative to last year. The figures are quite accurate, but people must nonetheless be told where those $200 million come from. A simple computation shows the 10 cents a pound increase on butter and the 2 cents a pound increase on powdered milk roughly account for the $200 million producers are granted by the minister.
All this boils down to this: the consumer foots the bill and the government goes scot free. Finally, there is a last area where the government did almost nothing, and this is controlling farm equipment prices. In my view the government should have done more, as regards both purchase prices and credit costs. I submit the minister should take note of this, and see to it that farmers in the future not lose their shirts buying equipment. And so it goes with the modernization required of the farmers. We are forever asking them to modernize and to do so they must borrow heavily without ever having the possibility of a reduced interest rate on the sum they have borrowed. I know that the Minister of Agriculture is not the only one to blame, this is rather a finance question. But I believe that with the help of the Minister of Agriculture we could increase our aid to farmers to make agriculture an even better paying proposition.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to thank the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) for moving the motion which is before us today, namely:
That this House deplores the government's inability to give leadership in developing and implementing comprehensive and co-ordinated agricultural policies and programs-
As my hon. friend from Medicine Hat said, most areas of the prairies are in a desperate situation because of lack of rainfall. The last rainfall in our district was last August, and the drought which began in August, 1976, in south central Saskatchewan now encompasses most of the region. There has been virtually no precipitation either of rain or snow since last August. It has been the driest winter since 1902. The area affected is large, covering virtually all the farmland in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, and a part of southeastern Alberta. I was in the Swift Current-Maple Creek district over the week end and when the aircraft in which I was travelling took off from Regina on Saturday it was not until we had reached 9,000 feet that it was above the dust pall hanging over the southern
Agriculture
prairies. Anyone who has lived in that area knows that May is the month when we get strong winds-this is surely the curse of the Palliser triangle.
Though the drought is as bad as it has ever been, fortunately, Mr. Speaker, our farming methods are greatly improved. Farmers can pretty well take anything mother nature throws at them; whether they can survive this government is a different question. The amount of money being expended on seeding the prairie crop is staggering. There must be at least $100 million worth of seed alone going into the ground, not to mention the cost of fuel, chemicals, wages, depreciation, and machinery repairs. Driving through the region one cannot help thinking that the greatest food reserve we have is the ability of our farmers and ranchers to continue to produce year after year. This is why it is so important, not only for the industry but for Canada and the world, that the federal government do everything possible to ensure a strong and viable agriculture.
One of the most annoying circumstances the producers face is the multitude of rules and regulations which flow from government and their departments almost extemporaneously, with almost no thought given to their consequences. Surely an industry such as agriculture which produces a saleable commodity should receive special attention. It is a direct responsibility of the government to ensure that the grain industry, which is so important to the strength of our exports and foreign exchange situation, should continue strong.
I think it behooves the government to take a look at the Rowell-Sirois report produced by that Royal Commission on Dominion-Provincial Relations which had its origins in the desperate situation of Western Canada in the thirties. The Commission said that Canada's most serious economic troubles in the thirties arose because of the impact of drought and world depression on the wheat growing industry of Saskatchewan. This industry, upon which the economic integration of the country was chiefly based, suffered the most unfavourable coincidence of circumstances in its history.
If the repercussions upon other sections of the Dominion were widespread and severe, conditions in Saskatchewan itself were nothing short of disastrous. Since, economically, this area was the most vulnerable in Canada, no other province was so dependent upon fluctuations in the export market. Nowhere was production so dependent upon the vagaries of the climate. The Commission reported that drought and ruinous prices were about equally responsible for the disaster and that the national economic policies of the Dominion did virtually nothing to soften the blow.
The main reason for the situation being so serious then, Mr. Speaker, is still with us today. It is that western agriculture is faced with such high fixed cost. I mentioned this earlier. I do not believe it is an exaggeration to say that this spring the total cost of getting the crop in will be a quarter of a billion dollars. The gravity of the situation is that for the grain farmer failure of a crop involves not merely the loss of livelihood but also the working capital which has been invested. Working capital has to be generated before the farmer gets another chance to become self-supporting.

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
Certainly conditions have changed since then and there are other safeguards undergirding western agriculture, for which we are grateful. But we still have to look back at the thirties, because for some three decades the expansion of our wheat industry had been a major factor in our prosperity, the growth of large incomes and the accumulation of wealth in some of the older regions of Canada. The province of Saskatchewan had no access, either by taxation or borrowing, to this surplus which its industry had created during prosperous times to tide it over years of adversity, so some transfer of income was absolutely essential to prevent widespread starvation in the province and the collapse of the wheat industry in those days. Thus the borrowing powers of the Dominion of Canada were used. Some things do not change, Mr. Speaker, and it is no wonder that the various regions of this country still look upon a centralist government in Ottawa with suspicion.
I sincerely hope, Mr. Speaker, that in the government's national emergency plan there is inclusion of drought measures. The only course of action in the short run is to concentrate on deep well drilling, pumping what surface water there is into town and farm dams and dugouts. Rain will not help our wells or dugouts this spring.
PFRA was set up in 1935 for two reasons, one being to alleviate soil drifting and the second to provide farm water supplies. That act has been a godsend. It seems to me that this measure has been allowed to run down over the years and what we are faced with now on an emergency basis should have been anticipated at least ten years ago. I cannot help looking at that South Saskatchewan irrigation project which has never really got off the ground. This year for the first time Lake Diefen-baker will not fill from the runoff of the South Saskatchewan River.
The most serious and immediate problem faces the ranchers, who even now are having to sell down their herds. As the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) said, almost half the cattle going to market now could be considered drought cattle and he suggested there should be some sort of tax deal for people who, through no fault of their own, are caught in a situation which requires them to sell down their herds on an emergency basis. The federal government must make available community pastures, even on an emergency basis, for feed and water. 1 am satisfied, however, that the PFRA people have the situation in hand as best they can, and that no cattle will have to leave community pastures because of a water shortage. However, the grass situation may be a different story. Surely means can be found to move feed into those pastures if necessary.
There is naturally great concern for cost factors in almost every area of agriculture. I will just take one, the marketing of our wheat over which producers have no control. The total operating costs of the Canadian Wheat Board for their pool account on wheat for 1975-76 as opposed to 1974-75 show a $35 million increase in the year. Total operating costs in the
1974-75 year were $68 million. Operating costs to the board

on their pool account for wheat in 1975-76 were over $103 million, a $35 million increase.
It does not seem to matter what item you look at, Mr. Speaker-bank interest, exchange and so on show an increase of 135 per cent. Country elevator administration charges increased by 60 per cent. Total carrying charges on the pool account for wheat went up 45 per cent in the last year.
Several days ago the Agricultural Institute of Canada appeared before our committee, and in their brief they said that declining expenditures on agricultural research and development cannot be claimed as part of the government's program of restraint initiated in late 1975. They said that the deterioration in research funding really began in 1969 and that it had continued without pause since then. It has been brought about through erosion by inflation. An average National Research Council operating grant in the biological sciences in
1974	was 6 per cent larger than in 1969; however, its purchasing power was 41 per cent less than in 1969. The Institute went on to deplore the lack of young Canadians entering our universities and research establishments, and said that in the United States there was a completely different picture, where bright young people were flocking to agricultural colleges, universities, and research centres.
Lack of federal support for research is going to mean that Canadian Wheat Board permit holders will be asked to vote this June on whether or not they should allow one tenth of one per cent of the elevator value of the six major grains to be set aside for research into production and grain marketing. Given last year's market, this would mean that $3.1 million would have been collected. It seems to me that the federal government has responsibility for basic research, transportation and export promotion, and probably more effort should be made here, with less attention being paid to our internal marketing systems.
An example of the great work turned out by our research scientists would be the new wheat "Sinton" which is the only red spring wheat resistant to leaf rust. I am pleased to say that this new variety, being grown commercially for the first time this year, was developed at the Agriculture Canada Swift Current research station. By all reports it is an excellent variety, no question about it.
In the Canadian Wheat Board annual report for 1975-76 the board talks about marketing problems encountered in the
1975	year. The report goes on to say that there were temporary holdbacks of sales lasting for two and a half months, from mid-August to the end of October, due to rain and tough grain. As it turned out, they say in their report, this came at a time when prices were at their high point in the crop year. By the time the results of the 1975 crop were known and the board was again able to go all out in sales efforts, prices had already started to decline.
It is pretty hard to explain to a producer why there would be a two and a half month halt in our selling operations when prices were at their peak. As I have said before, whereas bright young people are flocking into agriculture in the United States, the reverse seems to be true in Canada. These young
May 3, 1977

people know that other sectors of our economy have a basically rigid price structure which is especially resistant on the down side. This tends to steer them away from agriculture.
I have just been reading a report, Mr. Speaker, by Dr. W. A. Meneley, a geologist from Saskatoon. In his report he said that, in general, deeper observation wells, those greater than 100 feet in depth, do not display any pronounced seasonal water level change. Instead, they show a more subdued rise and fall in water level which reflects the longer term variations in the climate. The spring minimum water level trend in deep observation wells is above average and rising, in response to the generally favourable recharge conditions which have persisted in Saskatchewan during the past decade. Surely this is an area that deserves the immediate attention of the government.
It is these deep aquifers which provide the most reliable source of water supply available in southwestern Saskatchewan. Dr. Meneley says that ground water, even in deep aquifers, can be managed as a renewable resource. The immense storage capacity of our major aquifers can be drawn upon during dry years to provide essential water supply needs with the knowledge that the overdraft will be replenished by recharge when more favourable climatic conditions return again to the prairies.
In my own riding of Swift Current-Maple Creek we are sitting on top of a huge water resource. I hope that the Government of Canada puts all its effort into developing that resource. Water supply problems which will arise during 197778, Dr. Meneley says, can be resolved for the most part by providing incentives for developing deeper wells which are less affected by drought. The incentives should include provision for test drilling, electric logging to identify deeper aquifers, and support for well construction based on a percentage of the total well cost, including pumping equipment, rather than the fixed amount grant that is presently available from PFRA. The fixed grant creates a bias in favour of shallow well construction.
In southwestern Saskatchewan, where alternative surface water supply sources are lacking and no shallow aquifers are present, it may be necessary to construct very deep water supply wells, such as the 1,360 feet deep well that now supplies the village of Frontier. Such wells are very expensive and cost some $50,000 and up. That is the cost to drill and equip. This is beyond the financial capability of most individuals and most communities in that area. We are talking about a well that will pump 50 gallons a minute and up, or 15 million to 20 million gallons a year.
We are all hoping for good rains; but failing that the government has a responsibility. I suggest PFRA be brought back under Agriculture where it belongs; that a crash water program get under way; and that we have more research for basic agriculture. As I said before, my people can put up with almost anything mother nature wants to throw their way. How long they can put up with this government we will have to see.
Agriculture

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is a distinct pleasure for me to get involved in this debate this afternoon, especially a debate on the opposition's motion. It is a motion of non-confidence in agriculture. Having been involved in agriculture for over 40 years and having seen some of the difficulties in agriculture that we faced back in the thirties, in the forties, in the fifties-and I could go on-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: In the sixties and in the seventies.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: I am a little bit surprised that a motion of this type would come at a time like this when never before has the Government of Canada, under the direction of our present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), recognized agriculture to such an extent as one of the most important industries in this country.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Eugene Whelan wrote this speech. Wait and see how many times et cetera is said.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Agriculture, like never before, has been recognized.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Where?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Everywhere except in the opposition benches. Unfortunately I am surprised it has not had its recognition there. We, on this side of the House, have always recognized that fact. The minister has been a leader in this.
The agriculture sector generates substantial economic activity and creates employment in food marketing as well as in the agricultural and farm service industries. Almost 50 per cent of the people have jobs which are directly or indirectly related to agriculture, the food processing and producing industries in this country. Agriculture has been extremely efficient. In the last few years it has become so efficient that only 6 per cent of the people are directly involved in the production of agriculture. However, the fact that such a small proportion of the Canadian population is able to provide food for the rest of the country, and be a major world exporter of grain, is an indication of the strength and enormous productivity capacity of our agricultural industry.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Et cetera, et cetera.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: "Et cetera, et cetera", as the hon. member on the other side says.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: That is what the minister said.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
They have one enlightened member there, at least. I am appreciative of that. Our commitment to the world food aid program is well respected throughout the world. Canada is the largest contributor to the world food aid program in terms of actual dollars and commodities offered. For a country as sparsely populated as Canada, I am proud to be a member of that society. We export nearly $4 billion worth of agricultural products. Our balance of food is over a billion dollars.

I repeat the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture across Canada that our farmers are the most efficient in the world, and that each farmer in Canada can feed his family and 52 other Canadians. That is a record to be proud of, Mr. Speaker. That is something that is not being done in the rest of the world. In a country such as this, as the minister indicated earlier, it is efficient to provide food for that many people in Canada and throughout the rest of the world.
The government policy has been responsive to the needs of the agricultural industries. The government has recognized the problem experienced in the farming community in the face of great social and economic changes in the past decade. Government policy has consistently encouraged efficiency in farm operations. It has introduced and implemented programs for improvement and rationalization in the major areas of agricultural research, regional development, small family farm development, and domestic marketing. The main policy emphasis has been upon marketing and price levels of agricultural products, because the government understands that the viability of our food system is vital to our economic security both now and in the future.
We all recognize that agriculture is the basic industry in this country. A viable agricultural industry is basic to a viable economic structure of any nation. Our Minister of Agriculture has recognized this and has implemented policies to bring about just that. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when I was interrupted at six o'clock I was speaking about government policy on agriculture and the government's responsiveness to the needs of the agricultural industry. As always, the government's purpose is to serve the long time interest of the consumer, and that will remain so.
I should like to point out some of the initiatives that have been taken by this government. As was indicated earlier by a member on the other side of the House, the initiatives have not come from the opposition. It is the government that has been responsive to the needs of agriculture and this is recognized by the Minister of Agriculture.
In May of 1975 we had before us an amendment to the Farm Credit Act. This amendment enabled young farmers to get started in agriculture. They could borrow up to $150,000. Another major change allowed younger persons under the age of 35 to make a start in agriculture during a five year period.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: They now have a debt of $150,000 and they have no markets.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Let me tell the hon. member that I have been involved in agriculture for some time and I can well remember the time when one started in agriculture on a shoestring, and one stayed on that shoestring. But today young people come out of universities and out of various professions and can become involved in agriculture through assistance from the federal government.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: You should try it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I will tell the hon. member something. If he opened his eyes, he would see one of those people before him. I happen to have what I consider to be one of the most efficient agricultural operations anywhere in Canada, and I challenge anyone to compete with me. I am proud to have two of my sons, who have graduated in agriculture from the University of Guelph, operating that farm as efficiently as any in Canada. The hon. member says we do not have any markets. Because of some of the programs initiated by the government-I will be speaking about some of them a little later-we do have stable markets and we have a darn good idea of what will happen by the end of the year, provided we have a crop, and provided we do not have frost, and so on. This is the time of the year when we are susceptible to these kinds of disasters. But again the federal government has recognized this and has instituted programs to help us through these difficulties.
Another bill that was put forward and is at present before the House is to amend the Farm Improvement Loans Act, allowing the maximum limit on loans to be increased from $50,000 to $75,000. It takes considerable funds to run an agricultural business, and that is what it is today. We have certain input costs, but every efficient farmer can cover them at the end of the year.
We have the Stabilization Act which was amended in July of 1975 to provide greater assurance of market and price stability to farmers. The new act provides a set of programs for the major agricultural commodities in Canada which will give producers an effective stop-loss guarantee during periods characterized by market uncertainty or rapidly rising input costs. In 1976, under this program, support was given, as it related to my riding, for such commodities as sweet cherries, prune plums, and some varieties of pears. There seemed to be some difficulties in those areas and the federal government was there to support the farmer and help him through them.
The government has committed itself to measures which provide incentives for growth and stability in agriculture such as purchase programs under agricultural products boards. In times of critical need, the government has proven to be responsible.
I was personally involved in obtaining assistance for the sour cherry growers in 1975 when a surplus crop would have been left unharvested because the processor was not ready and willing to purchase it. It was through the Agricultural Products Marketing Board that the federal government purchased the surplus crop, froze it, and sold it the following year when
May 3, 1977

there was a light crop-and I might say, at a profit. The Agricultural Products Marketing Board stabilized returns by buying that crop, and thus the cost of the program was recovered and the producers saved from disaster. There was also an advantage to the consumer because in a light season supplies were available and prices did not skyrocket.
The program was also activitated for the peach crop even though the surplus was bought by the processors and the board was not required to make the purchase. We often find that processors and buyers play games with producers because they are dealing with a perishable commodity. It was not until the federal government stepped in and said it was ready to purchase the crop in my area that the processors purchased the crop, which up to that time had not been contracted for by them.
Last summer I was instrumental in the announcement of a federal support program for Ontario grapes. The federal Agricultural Products Marketing Board purchased some 7,000 tons of surplus grapes worth over $1 million to the growers in the Niagara Peninsula. Revenue from the sale of these products will offset the cost to the government.
Just to show what kinds of programs we have as opposed to some of the programs that some of the provinces, particularly the province of Ontario-

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Do not be partisan.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: I am not partisan, but I have to be fair and point this out.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Try to be truthful, too.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I am completely truthful, Mr. Speaker.
The federal government made an outright purchase of over 7,000 tons of grapes, while the program that the provincial government-and I am not quite sure what that program might be as I expect a drastic change in the provincial government very shortly-said, "We will guarantee a loan to the agency to buy some of the grapes." Mr. Speaker, they never put a nickel into that-they never took a chance on it. They said, "We will provide a loan to the farmers if they want to keep the grapes for a little while." The Minister of Agriculture however, said, "We will buy the grapes," with no strings attached.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Little old wine picker Gene.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Some of the crops in the horticultural industry are very perishable so the federal government has a program to assist in the construction of cold storage facilities to preserve them for an extended period. In 1975 18 projects were assisted at a construction cost of over $4 million, of which $500,000 went into a processing plant in the riding of Lincoln in the Niagara Peninsula. The effect of cold storage is to extend the season of perishable crops, which is in the interest of the consumer. The crops would otherwise go unharvested. I have seen cases where a crop matured very quickly but could not be processed. Because there were no cold storage facilities, the
Agriculture
Minister of Agriculture supported a program to assist them to the tune of $500,000.
From time to time we run into a problem with labour for the harvest even though, according to statistics and hon. members opposite, we have unemployment in this country. In agriculture, however, we find it difficult to get people to work at harvest time, so the federal government has responded by bringing in Caribbean agricultural workers to assist in the harvesting of perishables in Ontario and other provinces; but more specifically in the Niagara Peninsula. It seems that people here are a little better off than hon. members opposite sometimes indicate, and are not ready to do some of the stoop labour-that is what it is. When the weather gets a little warm it appears that our people do not want to work in the orchards so we have these other people come in to harvest the crops in order that they will not spoil. It has always been the objective of the Minister of Agriculture to make sure that all produce is harvested.
Another major factor has been legislation enabling orderly marketing schemes and supply management to bring stability to agricultural commodities. There has been much criticism of CEMA yet it has proven to be most beneficial not only in providing producers with a fair return on their investment according to a cost of production formula, but has also brought stability to the market with a guarantee of fresh quality products at fair prices to the consumer. The Minister of Agriculture pointed that out this afternoon when he spoke about the price of eggs, and I am sure hon. members will recognize the program has been extremely successful.
We also have a national turkey marketing agency and deliberations are going on at the present time with a view to establishing a national broiler plan. Some consumer groups in the country have been critical of such national schemes but I think it is very shortsighted for anyone, especially the consumer, to oppose them because they bring stability to the market place and assure the availability of food at modest prices.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Order, please. I regret to interrupt the hon. member but his allotted time has expired. He may continue, nevertheless, if there is unanimous consent.

speechtext: Agreed.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I thank you and hon. members, Mr. Speaker. I shall be very brief.
I should like to speak about the tariff board as it affects the Niagara Peninsula and the agricultural industry. Last week the Tariff Board released its findings in reference to fresh fruits and vegetables. Over all, it suggested moderate increased seasonal protection for Canada's 135,000 commercial growers and a safeguard against distress priced imports. These recommendations are based upon intensive study and representations made by the horticultural industry in Canada. I am very pleased with the recommendations made by this board, modest as they may be. Some of the reaction that I have seen in the news media, such as the heading, "Canadian consumer will now be faced with increased price for fruits and vegetables," is
80012-54%

totally erroneous. For the life of me I cannot understand how remarks like that are justified. Such remarks are irresponsible.
True, according to some statistics the price of fruits and vegetables has increased dramatically in the last few months, but I point out that such figures apply to fruits and vegetables not grown in this country. They are imported. The reasons given for the high prices are disasters such as bad weather in the country of origin. Mr. Speaker, fruit and vegetable prices increase in the off-season, but one always finds that they decrease when Canadian products come on the market. 1 am therefore pleased to note some of the recommendations made by the tariff review board.
Unfortunately, the tariff review board overlooked an item about which I shall make representation to the minister concerned. I am speaking of grapes. I understand the tariff review board overlooked that item and I shall make representation on behalf of my riding. One of our major crops is grapes. Mr. Speaker, I submit that Canadians need to be more aware of Canadian grapes and the products thereof. The quality of our grapes has improved dramatically. Some people still do not know this. I am sure that before long all Canadians will recognize how good are our grapes.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Our grapes and wines have won lots of awards lately.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Let me now say a word about research and development. Some hon. members have complained about the lack of research and development in agriculture. I say that new research facilities, new crop varieties, better methods of disease and insect control, and new farming techniques are accomplishments of the government's research branch. At Vineland in the Niagara Peninsula we have a unique sharing arrangement with the Ontario ministry of agriculture and food, under which emphasis is put on protection research. Provincial scientists carry out research on production of fruit and vegetable crops, and federal scientists are responsible for all protection research. Mr. Speaker, many times I recall gaining new knowledge and new insights from the people working at this station, particularly federal employees.
There are four federal research stations serving Ontario agriculture and funding has increased in the last five years from $6.6 million to $13.3 million. This amount represents approximately 10 per cent of the total annual research branch budget. At present 490 people staff the Vineland station, of whom 104 are scientists.
I have been pleased to put these facts on record to emphasize some of the things the federal government is doing. Speaking as one who is pleased to have an agricultural background, I am glad that my family still depends completely for its income from the primary production of the land. We know that as long as we have our present Minister of Agriculture, and as long as the federal government follows its present policies, we, and the consumers of Canada, shall remain in good hands.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the lot of any Minister of Agriculture of Canada can never be, by the very nature of the job, a happy one. No minister ever assumed responsibility for his portfolio with such good will, good will shown by farmers and members on all sides of the House, than was shown to the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). Yet the events of the last five years, particularly of the last three years, have forced Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition to move the motion the House is considering today. It deserves to be read time and again. It reads:
That this House deplores the government's inability to give leadership in developing and implementing comprehensive and co-ordinated agricultural policies and programs and regrets that by ill-advised and ad hoc remedies the government has weakened the over-all agricultural economy.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: To the Senate with Whelan.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Anyone who considers the history of agricultural policy of the last 40 years can make the case, I suggest, that never in the last 40 years has the agricultural industry been under such intensive attack by powers within the government as during the present. I speak not only of the powers within this government, but of those within provincial governments right across this country; indeed, I speak of governments around the world.
I suggest that nothing better demonstrates my point than the rhetoric in the amendment to the motion proposed by the New Democratic Party. Let me read the amendment to the motion proposed by the party which once used to stand up for agriculture. It reads:
and this House further regrets the government's failure to give full support to an orderly marketing system which would give producers the collective strength to reduce corporate power in the food system and stabilize farm incomes as well as prices to consumers.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: What's wrong with the amendment?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: What's wrong with it? The hon. member's party has proposed the very policies which have put agriculture on the defensive. That party's amendment would take the decision-making power out of the hands of producers and put it into the hands of bureaucrats. It would let bureaucrats take the farmer by the throat and increasingly push him into the ground.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Shame on the NDP.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no party has a stronger, longer record of support for orderly marketing than Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition, the Conservative party. My party put on the statute books of this nation the Natural Products Marketing Act in 1934. That was 43 years ago. We did it to give producers some control over their own destiny. What has happened since the war is this: bureaucrats, mandarins, call them what you will, have fought to take over the direction of marketing boards. Their purpose has not been to make them into instruments to expand the market and increase the farmer's income. Their purpose has
May 3, 1977

been to use them as instruments of the civil service with which to control and curb the decision-making powers of the farmer.
In the last number of years we have witnessed the government, speaking through its civil servants in Ottawa, interfering with the independence of the Canadian Wheat Board. I know the history of the Canadian Wheat Board. The original act was passed in this House in 1935. It was opposed by the Liberals in opposition. In 1939 the then Liberal government introduced four bills which would have got rid of the Canadian Wheat Board. Those bills were passed but not put into effect, because war broke out. The civil service realized that in the Wheat Board it had a device with which it could control the price to the farmer, and that is why the Wheat Board was saved.
After the war, by virtue of the British wheat agreement, our wheat prices were controlled at a time when world wheat prices were high. The wheat industry was controlled long after the ordinary citizen in Canada was freed from controls. I have seen this gradual encroachment on power of the so-called and self-styled leaders of opinion, of this managerial elite, of people who think they know better how to run this country than do the elected members of parliament. The NDP amendment would have us all walk into the trap of turning power over to the bureaucrats.
This evening I will not go so far as to lay blame for what has happened on the minister. I have expressed my feelings for the minister in the Standing Committee on Agriculture. He knows that Conservative members serving on that committee have tried to expand the control of the Minister of Agriculture over those institutions of government which are properly concerned about agriculture.
What has happened to ARDA today? That is the one device which would have helped the people of Thunder Bay, Algoma, the Ottawa Valley, northern Quebec, northern Ontario, and all the other agriculturally depressed areas. ARDA was to be their main line of attack for raising their income. Where is it now? Is it under the minister? I do not blame that on the minister. I blame it on a government that has sold its soul to the mandarins.
Where is the PFRA that was passed by this House in 1935 to rehabilitate the dried out deserts of the prairies which now produce half the agricultural wealth of this country? Where is the PFRA? Is it under the minister? It is under another minister. The shame of it all! Now when we are again in our moment of need, as we always will be with these periodic droughts in the west, our Minister of Agriculture is unable through his own department to take that organization, which is a federal organization which all the provinces in the west have agreed would have the priority in handling drought problems, and have jurisdiction over it.
Where is the crop insurance? Where is the PFAA? We have a bill in this House to get rid of it because crop insurance made it obsolete. Why does the bill stay before the House? It is because we caught the political machine of one of the
Agriculture
minister's colleagues monkeying around in the PFAA. The head man appointed by that minister was up before the courts on criminal fraud. After the judge heard the preliminary evidence, he said that man would be tried. However, the trial has never taken place. The finger of responsibility always has to come back to the minister who holds the responsibility, the Minister of Agriculture. All the Minister of Agriculture could do last year was to get up in the House and say the trial has not taken place. But his civil servants have burned all the papers, burned all the records. Why were all those secretaries fired a month before Christmas when they had not done anything wrong? Why were they fired when parliament voted for them to continue work until the end of March that fiscal year? It was because that machine did not want parliament to ask any more questions.
It came out in answer to a question by the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) recently that money which belongs to the farmers has not collected any interest for the past three years. You can understand why farmers all across the country are asking what is going on here.
Why was it necessary for 5,000 Quebec dairy farmers to come onto on the grounds of these buildings last year? When the minister held out his hands and said "Mes amis, I am your Minister of Agriculture", they responded with an attack of milk bottles that he knows all about. When those same farmers went to the polls on November 15 last and voted separatist, they knew that somebody here was not working on their side.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: The dairy industry is under the hands of the mandarins, that small group of bureaucrats who think they know how to run a cow. They make quotas they hope will satisfy. They think they can plan grain, grass, and breed the cows to give the right amount of milk. Those nitwits could not fight their way out of a paper bag on a misty day.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I could go on and on and take point after point. In 1969 these bright boys got together and produced a thick volume known as the task force report. What did these great minds of Canada say? These people who did that task force report for the Liberal government of that day said there were three times too many farmers in Canada and the only way to help them was to cut them down to one third of that number. Boy, did they try! This government rushed into the breach. It put in the Lift program for the prairies. Lower inventories for tomorrow turned out to be lower incomes for tomorrow. It took us out of wheat production at a time when the world was going into one of its worst droughts in history.
A few months later the minister put the wheat price down and dumped wheat on the market. That is when I labelled him "Firesale Otto". When we said, "Please get the price up because we have not got the wheat", he replied that the experts said that there were 500 million bushels hidden on the

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
farms. Boy, what a mouthful those rabbits had to swallow! When they went to get the wheat in 1972, there was no wheat and the price went up to over $5 a bushel.
I would like to believe it was only our mistake in Canada, but the same thing happened to United States farmers. At the time they were negotiating with the Russians at the same price we were charging in our firesale operation, no one believed the farmers when they said there was no wheat. When they went to get it to meet the Russian sale, they could not find it.
The American farmers were very angry. We know what farmers do when they are angry. They did the same thing in the United States as they are going to do in some of these by-elections in Quebec. Those farmers are going to try to scare heck, not out of the Minister of Agriculture, but out of the government that does these awful things to them.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Have we taken a beating! Three years ago as the drought came up the central plains from the Gulf of Mexico, we could see we were moving from the wet to the dry part of the cycle. With timely rains we grew a good crop in 1975 and a better crop in 1976. Then what happened? The wheat board said, "We have no more grains to sell," and quit selling. That was in June, 1976. In September-October, they rushed out and made a deal to sell 200 million bushels of grain at $1 below the real price. According to the contract, the people who bought did not even have to pay for it in the sense of taking delivery of the wheat. They do not have to take delivery until August 1 of this year.
Somebody has to pay for the storage. Guess who that will be? The farmer. Somebody has to pay the interest on the money that was borrowed to make the advance payment on that wheat. Guess who will pay that? Right, the farmer. He cannot be blamed for wondering why they are attacking him all the time.
The price is away down. All we have had is public relations ever since that time to prove that the price should be down. In spite of that, the price keeps going up. Meanwhile, these people may take a dollar's profit out of their grain.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: The price has been going down for a year. Where have you been?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) is a little confused some of the time. This is one of those times. If he looked at the records, he would know the price was down to $4.15 to $4.20 a bushel. The Rotterdam price has been moving up in spite of this propaganda.
Today we are in a period of drought. Sure enough our beef farmers are the first line of attack about anything being done, but the grain farmer knows that he has to meet this situation. He knows that with all this money spent for planting the grain, and knowing that the wheat price is also lower than last year, he will not get any more. He knows he will not have too much

this year, even if the rains do come. He cannot help wondering what is going on here.
If anyone wants to take the time to read the speeches this afternoon of the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) and the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton), they will see they were not begging speeches. They put on the record the heart-felt feelings of grain farmers who had got on their feet in 1974 and 1975 and had been going ahead. All of a sudden they were slapped down in 1976, and now they face this drought in 1977.
I would like to make my concluding remarks, to stay within my time limit, on this question of drought. We have in the official records of the Department of Agriculture going back to 1875 the amount of rainfall we get every year. Also in that department we have the average production of wheat every year. Every Minister of Agriculture who is representing the farmer should have on his wall a chart of the rainfall and the production so that he knows when we are going into the drought cycles and when we are coming out of them. But since the present Minister of Agriculture is not even allowed to look after wheat, he has to take the information from his colleague. In 1961 we experienced the worst drought in Canada's history, and when the farmers asked for help, it was ready.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Two hundred bucks!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
When the farmers asked for help the provincial governments of Alberta and Saskatchewan and Manitoba recommended to the federal government that we should slaughter a million and a half head of beef cattle. That was the recommendation of the civil servants of Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta in the year 1961. The federal government refused to take that advice, went back to the provincial ministers-not their deputies-and said, "Here is a 17 point program to meet that drought." It said to the farmers, "After you have done all you can, if you cannot get the feed to feed your cattle we will feed them No. 1. wheat; if you move them out to the pastures we will feed them." Out of six million head, only 7,000 head appeared. The farmers fought like tigers because they knew the government was ready to feed the cattle if they failed.
With regard to the water question we moved pumps and pipes from every part of Canada, and when any farmer asked for his well to be filled or his dugout to be filled, pumps were put in and his well was filled. That is why the people of Saskatchewan, in spite of all the propaganda they hear from the NDP, put in Conservatives in federal elections in Saskatchewan. They know who stood by them.
