speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is sad that a certain hon. member of this House has refused to let my predecessor finish his speech since I do believe it would have brought back something of our past, almost reaching out to ancient times, that is, when he was himself Minister of Agriculture.
Well, Mr. Speaker, nowadays everyone tries his best to defend certain positions or criticize the agricultural field or its minister or the government itself. First of all, I quarrel with the wording of the motion. It is proposed in terms that are accepted by this august assembly but as far as I am concerned, the wording does not quite correspond to reality. The motion is presented by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), one of my good colleagues, who I know has the necessary ability to discuss the agriculture issue, in fact or in practice, since he has been involved in the same kind of agriculture I have myself practiced in the past and has himself suffered as I did when his own party was in power. That is why I grant that it is possible for him to introduce a no-confidence motion.
Agriculture
The motion says "this House deplores" but it is not really the House, Mr. Speaker; when we speak of the House of Commons, we think of all the political parties and right now I feel that only a very small group, not even half the members of the opposition, could deplore something that they know nothing about in the agricultural activities of the last few years, but possibly they might deplore something that has not been done.
I endorse this last possibility. As for the wording itself, I reject it and accept, for example, that regardless of our political conviction, the democratic principles allow us to declare openly at any time that the laws of this country do not correspond to reality or could correspond to it or should be improved upon. But no matter to which party we belong, any responsible member, whether on this side of the House or on the other, must admit that we did not do what we should have done in due time in committees, when we were in power, or what we should say to the government when we are not in power. That is why I think it is unfortunate that our farmers run their farms the way various MPs or MLAs discharge their own duties. I feel many more farmers would go bankrupt, Mr. Speaker. I think this is illogical. I seldom rise in the House. Why? Because I think that the legislator's role is primarily to draft bills which can meet the future needs of farmers, and very often we are not able ourselves to plan for the future because we cannot foresee it. I often notice in the House, on this side or the other, that easy solutions are found: When it is raining, it is easy to say that we should call in the sun. When the sun shows up, the opposition usually claims credit for it. When the weather is bad, this government has summoned the clouds.
Mr. Speaker, I have discussed a few points but not for the sake of demagoguery or position. That is not my purpose because, to my mind, it would be destructive. It certainly is not constructive to attack this one or that, without suggesting solutions. We are not elected for that. When an elector in our riding makes his little cross on his ballot to send a member to the legislative assembly of his province or to the House of Commons of his country, he is confident the man for whom he has voted is more serious than that.
Mr. Speaker, I heard criticism a while ago, but nothing positive with regard to the government, except when the minister tried to explain certain points. But, according to the opposition, nothing has been done; yet, it makes no suggestions. I though I would be able to emphasize each point, Mr. Speaker. The speeches of each hon. member who took the floor can show us how serious these people are. My colleague the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise) had nothing but criticism. However, I admit he can do better than what he showed the House this afternoon. I would have thought he could have proposed solutions to genuine problems. So, Mr. Speaker, if time permits I would like to attempt to submit solutions which the present government should study, even if I were one of its members. This is the kind of suggestion I was expecting from the hon. member for Elgin.
As far as the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) is concerned, he expressed a view which I found

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
extremely disappointing. However, only twice did he attend the meetings of the Committee on Agriculture relating to the last budget and he blamed the government for pouring too much money in the budget, and the Minister of Agriculture was blamed in committee. Yet this afternoon we saw the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville say to the minister that there should be more money put in the budget for research. You have to be consistent. Either you tell the House that there is not enough money and you vote the supplies in committee or you ask the minister to put in more. Or you refuse in committee to put money in such and such an area of agriculture and, back in the House, you say the same thing. You have to be consistent.
Mr. Speaker, I will leave all that aside. The dairy policy is the last point I will attempt to deal with. The hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier) already talked about it. I do not have the time, because it goes by too quickly, to take up his challenge. I refer to what was said by the hon. member who spoke before me, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton). I heard some pretty good ones a while ago!
Mr. Speaker, in 1957, 1958, 1959, 1960, 1963, I came here to Ottawa as a representative of the farmers' association and at that time the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain was Minister of Agriculture. He cried over our shoulders earlier suggesting that he was not happy with the present agricultural system and the 5,000 farmers who came before Parliament last spring. The mover was, as I was, a milk producer in 1957 when milk was selling at $3.25 per hundredweight. If I mention that, that is merely talking about ancient times but I would like people to be aware of what they suggest in the House. That is reported in Hansard and will remain there. Irresponsible words should not be spoken as if nobody could go back and read them over. That is serious.
In 1957, the mover and 1 were selling milk at $3.25 per hundredweight and I do not dissociate myself from the farmers at that time. Collectively, we said that the government was not a good government because at that time the Progressive Conservative party offered us much more than we were supposed to have. Then, we supported collectively all Canadian farmers and we endorsed the opinions put forward at that time. Six years later, Mr. Speaker, any farmer who produced about 300,000 lbs. of milk had suffered a loss of income. That is what the Progressive Conservative party proposed to us, they promised us the moon and we did not even get a star because we had lost 56 cents per hundredweight of milk. Over six years, it was a regressive increase, a decreasing increase.
Yet, some ministers of agriculture at the time will now have us believe that everything is wrong because the present government has favoured 5,000 farmers. At that time, I came here to submit briefs, but nobody understood us. The agriculture budget, which was split about 50-50 between eastern and western Canada, has been shifted, and I am pleased to see that western farmers have gained by it, but 65 per cent of the agriculture budget has been shifted to three provinces of Canada and 65 per cent of the farmers now share 35 per cent

of the budget. Today, nothing has been reduced in western Canada and let somebody prove to me that the western producers' income from wheat, oats, feed grain or export grain has decreased. There has been no decrease, but now a balance has been struck in eastern Canada. There is no more for one than for the other, but there is a sort of balance, but at what cost?
Mr. Speaker, when milk producers came here last year to blame the government for being the victims of a democratisa-tion process carried too far. Many years ago, in the province of Quebec, someone created a sort of myth known as autonomy. Autonomy should have allowed a provincial government to have jurisdiction over a great number of Canadian pieces of legislation, but under that autonomy, some powers have been transferred over which we have lost control, and now that control is in the hands of the producers' associations of which I have been a member myself.
I am happy that they are taking over providing they handle it properly. Unfortunately, that happened last year. In the case of opposition members, however, I see the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) in the background and I feel he should be aware of the situation. If he had gone through what I experienced, he might be discomforted by certain attempts at criticism from his colleagues. He would realize that Quebec has no need at this point for criticism, but rather for understanding. If we throw problems at one another, we will find no solutions. But solutions are needed as regards the dairy policy which accounts for 48 per cent of the national production. Last year, the cost to the Canadian government of that policy was higher than in any other country, including the European Economic Community. Figures show that the cost to the Canadian government for this same commodity of the dairy policy was higher than the overall EEC budget for the whole
1975-76 fiscal year, because the EEC has no direct subsidy on the hundredweight of milk. The Americans next door could give farmers nothing more than $2.35 short of what our farmers got here. Admittedly, this is not enough, and I look forward to having more and more, just like our farmers do. But as far as saying that everything is wrong, this is another story. We must be rational about this. Whatever is given must come from somewhere. That is the name of the game.
I therefore ask the opposition members who introduced this non-confidence motion and who have contributed to this debate when they have allowed us to increase the budget of such and such a department. They have always criticized the budget of each department, and when they make some minor criticism, often it is not about the budget, but about the administration. We are criticized for not granting even more money. If there were farmers to hear us in the gallery, I think we would be ashamed.
I said earlier that the producers would get into trouble if we were to administer the country in this way or if we wasted our time as we are now doing. I submit that I can achieve nothing by doing what I now have to do. According to the rules, the leader of the House had to grant an opposition day and the opposition had to find a subject of debate, whether it was
May 3, 1977

justified or not. I find this deplorable and a waste of time. But I think that if we do not want Canada to face serious consequences or our producer organizations to face administrative failures because of our dairy policy, we shall have to be more serious on both sides of the House and we shall have to describe the problems as they really are so that Quebecers will not imagine that things are as bad as all that in Ottawa.
When they play these little games, the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Wagner) or the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle)-who are well aware of the situation in Quebec and who can understand what is going on because they know what separatism is like as they have left certain political parties themselves-harm me as a Quebecer, they harm the various farm producers, because they are using a philosophy which has no bearing on Canadian policies. When this happens, what I heard earlier is repeated. 1 found what the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) said unfortunate. This is ridiculous and some will say later on: It is the fault of the central government if the situation is so serious in Quebec.
Let us not forget the $632 million invested in agriculture last year. No one is aware of this in Quebec. Even if we talk about this investment, the few members of the opposition say that it is not true. The farmer does not know if it is true or not. If they say we did not do enough, if they criticize us for not getting enough money from taxes, I am ready to accept it because the government does not give anything, it only redistributes wealth.
How many members from my province have been able to explain the efforts aimed at making our agricultural costs competitive with those of other countries? How many members from my province have been able to say to what extent the problems caused by the weather in our regions are reduced owing to the hundreds of millions paid by the government of Canada? Nobody mentioned that. How many people have heard about the protection given to farm product marketing by a bill, the famous Bill C-176 that cost a lot of money.
Mr. Speaker, I tend to look at the hon. member for Joliette as he is about the only one that can understand me as he speaks French. At that time, it was sad to see what was happening to some members of the opposition. One of them joined us and we must convince him about those bills and show him that we wanted an orderly marketing of farm products for agricultural associations but it took us two years to pass the legislation, this is unfortunate and now that this bill comes back to the House, it is criticized. If we play into the hands of some farmers, who do not realize the value of those bills, we shall do the same thing as the hon. member for Joliette and the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe.
We shall do the same thing as some hon. members who ignore under which legislation they were sent. They wish to serve their political ends, to make speeches while newsmen
Agriculture
listen to us to report it in the press. Those people do not sit on the Committee on Agriculture. I do not see them there. As my allotted time is probably expired, I shall end my comments.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to join in the debate in support of the motion of the official opposition which in effect deplores the government's inability to give leadership in developing and implementing comprehensive and co-ordinated agricultural policies and programs. My remarks will be relatively brief because I understand there are one or two other speakers, both on this side and the other side, who wish to make a few comments.
Under the British North America Act, with respect to agriculture the powers are divided between the provinces and the federal authorities. The provincial governments have powers to make laws or to pass legislation within their boundaries. The federal government, of course, has the power as well to pass legislation dealing with agriculture within the provinces. That power given to the federal government has an overriding authority over the provincial legislatures. Under these circumstances it seems to me that it is important, where there is an overlapping or a combination of authority, that there be a maximum of co-operation between the two levels of government-the departments of agriculture of the various provinces and of the federal government. If we have that degree of co-ordination and co-operation, we end up with a well-functioning agricultural industry.
Basically the provincial authorities, the provincial governments, are much closer to the grass roots. I would suggest that they have a greater appreciation of the problems of agriculture within their boundaries. There should be a constant flow of information passing back and forth between the provincial authorities and the federal authorities in order that there be a better understanding of the problems respecting agriculture. This is not always so. There is not always this degree of co-operation or understanding. There are a number of reasons for that. One of them perhaps is politics-the fact that a provincial government is of a different stripe than the federal government. There is a question of power in the bureaucracy, and there is a question of clash of personalities.
The business of livestock comes to mind. That was a case and is a case where there have been problems in the livestock industry for some considerable time. In the livestock industry and in considering its problems, there was no co-operation and very little, if any, consultation between the federal and the provincial authorities. It seems to be that each of the provinces wants its own way. First of all, there was a feeling based on faulty statistics that there was a shortage of cattle in the country. The provinces encouraged the livestock producers to increase their herds. They gave them interest free loans and so

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
on. Suddenly they found there was overproduction, and each province discovered it had to start its own stabilization program to help its producers keep in business. You can see the mess the livestock producers are in today.
I blame the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) because he should have been aware of this situation. If he was not aware, it was a case that he was not consulting with his provincial counterparts. He finally did assess the situation. I believe this, because he was asked questions in this House from time to time and the situation was explained to him. But he stalled and stalled, and the result was that each province went its own way. The minister failed to analyse the situation properly.
One of the problems that arose was the question of the importation of offshore beef. Despite the fact that the provinces and the livestock producers had been telling the Minister of Agriculture that the importation of offshore beef was a problem, he delayed action until it was too late. As I said, it is important, if we are to have a sound agricultural industry, that there be co-operation. Some time ago the government moved the responsibility for PFRA from the Ministry of Agriculture to the Ministry of Regional Economic Expansion. PFRA falls within the purview of the Minister of Agriculture. I am not suggesting that the present Minister of Agriculture was responsible for having PFRA moved to DREE.

PFRA was set up in 1935 by the government of R. B. Bennett, a Conservative government, and its purpose was to assist in the reclamation of agricultural lands that were seriously affected by drought and soil drifting in the prairies in the 1930's.

PFRA responsibilities were later extended to include water conservation and development, land use adjustment, large scale irrigation, reclamation, community pastures, and so on. PFRA was instrumental in the construction of the Gardiner dam on the Diefenbaker Lake, which has added greatly to the province of Saskatchewan and to the agricultural industry. We have an irrigation scheme in the Outlook area. An hon. member opposite says "What is wrong with that?" There is nothing wrong with that. The dam was built by a Conservative government. A former minister of agriculture for

years was elected to the House on the promise of building a dam. That was his province, and finally when the Conservative government put foward the motion to build the dam, he voted against it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS

speechtext: They both promised it for 50 years.

speechtext: I accept the hon. member's statement regarding what he has said. I heard him in passing and I assumed he was making a detrimental comment, so I wanted to put him straight.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Not at all.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: A plague on both houses.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: After the dam was built, the federal government never followed through with its plans. The plan was that the irrigated area in central Saskatchewan around the Outlook area would be extended. There was an agreement with the province of Saskatchewan, but for one reason or another-one of the main reasons being lack of communication and co-operation between the two governments-the irrigation area was never extended. It would be a godsend today in Saskatchewan if the irrigation area around the Diefenbaker Lake had been extended.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: There ain't no water in it.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
I think one of the basic reasons was that the bureaucrats who were running the department forgot the lessons of the 1930's. They lacked foresight and they failed to understand the need for water. If PFRA had been allowed to function as it was originally intended, if the government had given its support to it and had left it within the jurisdiction of the Department of Agriculture, I suggest that many of the drainage areas in Saskatchewan, Manitoba and Alberta would have been developed in order to make water supplies available for some of the towns and cities in the prairies, and for irrigation purposes, because PFRA had the top expertise in Canada as far as water drainage and land development in Canada was concerned. But once PFRA was shifted to DREE, it went down. As the honourable member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) said, it is now in the hands of the undertaker.
In closing I would like to make one or two brief comments on the amendment of my friends to the left to change the period at the end of the main motion to a comma, and add the following words:
-and this House further regrets the government's failure to give full support to an orderly marketing system which would give producers the collective strength to reduce corporate power in the food system and stabilize farm incomes as well as prices to consumers.
May 3, 1977

They talk about full support to an orderly marketing system. Our party does not support the amendment put forward by the NDP. We are not opposed to the principle of marketing boards, provided they are producer controlled and set up in a democratic manner by producers. We do not believe in the supply management concept such as suggested by my friends to the left who would like to see the agricultural industry and every other industry in Canada controlled by the bureaucrats. We cannot go along with that concept. We believe in a democratic society where the producer is allowed to make up his mind. For that reason, and to give other honourable members an opportunity to speak, I will conclude by saying that we cannot support the undemocratic amendment of the NDP.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to be taking part for a few moments in this debate following the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil).
It is interesting to note again, in a motion put today by the official opposition dealing with agriculture, that this is another excellent example of how completely devoid they are of any constructive ideas. The only constructive thing in the debate so far is that it has been helpful in highlighting the possibility of drought in western Canada. To their credit, the two members who did such a good job, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) and the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton), did not blame the government for this, as I am sure some of their colleagues would have done. That has certainly been the only positive aspect of today's debate.
Hon. members opposite were again carping and critical and harking back to the 1930's and 1950's when they were last in power, with the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) reciting the litany of his achievements. I will say he had a number of achievements to his credit, but since that time his party has been devoid of any agricultural policy and today's debate proved that again. They are critical of this government, of the minister's efforts, and of his tremendous success in dealing with the problems of food production and the food producers in Canada. I can only assume they are envious of the minister and his record.
My good friend, the hon. member for Medicine Hat, who took part in the debate before the supper hour, made an excellent contribution. He made one statement, however, with which I wish to take some exception unless I misheard him. He was concerned about the abnormally high incomes producers might be receiving for beef cattle if they were forced to market them by virtue of the drought conditions. I would say that with the record of returns to beef producers over the last three or four years they are not going to have abnormally high returns; indeed they may have a tax liability.
If the hon. member can name ten cattle producers in western Canada with an income tax problem, I will be glad to produce 1,000 names of people who have a much more serious
Agriculture
negative income problem. I am not saying that there should not be reforms in tax laws as far as the beef industry is concerned, but certainly it is not an urgent priority in terms of legislation to improve income averaging.
Over the past four years or nearly four years, the beef producer has suffered financial losses, the magnitude of which we have probably never seen before and will hopefully not see again. The reasons are complex and the solutions are complex. Unlike some others I do not propose or suggest that I have any simple or magic answers. There are a great many myths and a great many simple answers that have been put forward, not only in this debate but in other circles. We heard the hon. member for Moose Jaw mention that provincial government assistance programs guarantee loans. In the case of the government of Saskatchewan and the government of Alberta a few years ago, some said this was the cause of the downturn in the western Canadian beef industry. This kind of charge is untrue and has nothing whatever to do with the broader basic problems of world over-supply and North American over-supply that brought about the chaotic marketing conditions we have witnessed.
There are those who say that when this government came out with the seven cents per pound premium, later scaled down to five cents, then three cents, and eventually phased out, it created a drop in beef prices which upset the market. The fact of the matter is that the Omaha market was dropping, and no matter what the government or the producers of Canada did they were faced with a downturn in the American market which our market generally follows. It is true that over the last three or four years generally our market has dropped to the same degree. Even last year while the critics were blaming the "down under" beef imports from Australia and New Zealand for causing the problems in the Canadian market, the fact of the matter was that finished beef in Canada was generally priced two or three cents above the Omaha price. Even while a great deal more beef was imported from Australia and New Zealand last year, at the same time more ground beef left this country for the United States.
There are those who say that government intervention is the cause of problems in the beef industry in Canada. They want no government help; they say they do not need government help. What surprises me is that these are quite often the same people who have very large leases of Crown pasture land or are perhaps enjoying the publicly funded water conservation program of the PFRA or the patronage of PFRA pastures or provincial community pastures. The rates for all these are generally much below those of producers who own their land. In my part of Saskatchewan the majority of cattle producers do own their land as opposed to the case in southern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta. I have always been interested to hear people say, "We do not need any government help or intervention; keep giving us the things we enjoy, the benefit of the taxpayers' money."
We hear some people say that a marketing board with broad supply management powers would resolve our beef marketing difficulties, and I am aware that the Minister of Agriculture

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
(Mr. Whelan) strongly believes in that principle. The only problem with this is that the majority of western Canada beef producers simply do not share or support that view. The minister has repeated that any such proposal would only come about with the democratic and majority support of producers. I am glad to hear him say that, but I say to him that such support may come about eventually. In my view, however, it will be many years down the road before producers will make that decision on their own. I would need a lot more evidence than has been available so far.
In the meantime I suggest we should set aside the debate on "whether or not the marketing board," and instead the minister should continue working in those areas where there is support for development of a better consensus to help the beef producers of this nation. There are some areas where there is pretty general consensus which my friends in the New Democratic Party can certainly support.
There is little doubt that beef producers today, regardless of their philosophical views on marketing, or their political views, are prepared to recognize there is a serious problem and are prepared to work out solutions. It is generally agreed that improved information service to the producers about numbers, supplies, kinds of cattle and so on, and information about the industry in this country, the United States and elsewhere, would enable them to make their own decisions. There is little doubt in my mind or that of anybody associated with the industry for any length of time, that we need increased research into disease control and disease prevention. Every year we are still losing unnecessarily tens of thousands of dollars because calves and cattle of all sizes and ages are afflicted with diseases which have been with us for many years. We are making little progress to control or prevent these diseases.
Third, and related to that, we also need funds to support more and better veterinary preventive medical programs, which should be made available through provincial governments to producers on a cost-shared basis. Money spent on such a program would be of direct benefit not only to the producer but to the consumer as well, because it would increase and improve the efficiency of our industry.
Fourth and finally, it seems to me that we need more and better co-ordination among federal departments and agencies dealing with beef. In this respect I am thinking of some structure similar to the grains group which was set up by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Oh, no!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: My hon. friend opposite says, "oh, no!" However, by setting up that group the minister brought together all those government agencies dealing with grain and allowed them to focus their attention on grain, including the transportation and marketing of grain.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: And you are still not getting a good deal.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That, I think, should be our approach with respect to the beef industry. We should make sure there is greater co-ordination of the activities of federal agencies dealing with beef, so that each agency will know what the other is doing in fields of marketing, grading, production, export and so on.
I think the Minister of Agriculture has done a tremendously good job in going across this country and speaking to many hundreds of producers in all parts of Canada. As I say, he has spoken to producers in almost every corner of the country. I know that it has been difficult for him and others to arrive at any definite consensus with respect to the beef industry, particularly in view of the problems that industry has gone through in the past several years, but I believe that today we are closer to arriving at a consensus with respect to the needs of the industry.
It is obvious to me, to beef men and farmers right across this country, that the minister has made tremendous efforts to meet farmers, talk to them, and learn about their problems. He implemented in the beef industry a finished beef stabilization program which has been of great help. That program was improved again this year. Provision was made for four quarterly payments which will more accurately reflect changes in the market.
At the turn of the year the minister was able to announce a cow-calf stabilization program which will be effective this year. Like the hon. member for Medicine Hat I would welcome the opportunity to discuss this program at greater length. The program represents a beginning. I hope market conditions this fall will be such as to make the program unnecessary. On the other hand lam happy to see that program in place. It will be of benefit if the market place does not increase prices. We must try to make that program effective and workable and I suggest that can be done if co-operation in this respect is shown.
In another debate I intend to take exception to certain remarks made by the former minister, the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain, relating to some insinuation and charges he made in this debate. If they are anything like as serious as he intimated, the matter should be brought directly to the attention of the attorney general of Saskatchewan. But I know the hon. member is not prepared to do that. I should like to discuss that matter at greater length in another debate.
We know what Tory policy is.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: No, you don't. What is it? The Tories themselves don't know.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: We know primarily what it is. They made their policy clear in today's debate.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Do you know the NDP's policy?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Yes, I think we know it. What is Tory policy? First, it is that there shall be no government intervention of any kind. Second, they say, leave the working of agriculture entirely to the open market or the market place. One should
May 3, 1977

define those terms, because I am not exactly sure what they mean. Third, they say, open all the borders, even though in 1975 hon. members opposite asked the Minister of Agriculture to close the border. Fourth they want no beef stabilization program of any kind. That has been the Tory policy. They want no grain stabilizaion program of any kind. They oppose the plan now in place. I could go on listing the negative aims and objects in agriculture of the official opposition.
Let me conclude on a positive note by saying that the party opposite made certain constructive suggestions when highlighting the seriousness of the drought in western Canada. Let me say, as well, that PFRA and other agencies operating in the area will certainly respond to demands and programs which may be put in place. I believe the Minister of Agriculture himself is now discussing such programs with ministers of agriculture of western Canada, as well as with premiers. I assure hon. members opposite that the government, PFRA, the Minister of Agriculture and others responsible will respond, if the need to do so arises. Contrary to what the hon. member for Moose Jaw suggested, PFRA is in place. It is performing its function and ready to carry out its responsibilities. It still has the necessary expertise, and the organization will do the job if it is asked to do it in the next few weeks.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Thanks a lot. I will remember that.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to speak only to the amendment. I was surprised to hear hon. members on my right reciting history. It is apparent that the Conservatives never look forward. They only look back. I heard a great recital of what they had done but the fact is they did little. Actually they have opposed for some time practically every constructive piece of legislation which has come forward.
I was amused to hear western Conservatives praising Jimmy Gardiner's PFRA army, considering that they fought unsuccessfully for years to get rid of him.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Progressive Conservative Party Deputy House Leader
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: I think the hon. member is speaking about PFAA. Does he not know the difference?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture presented a brief today; in it those representatives of farmers said among other things the following:
Farmers are however disturbed by calls for a 'national food policy', as if we didn't have one, and as if the body of existing policy in this country presented a scene of widespread disarray. This is not so.
One can see why we proposed the amendment to the motion. We wanted to cure some of the problems which have developed in the west as a result of archaic thinking. It is apparent that some people are not willing to face the problems of the beef industry. If there was ever an industry that needed help, it is the beef industry. If there was ever a time when the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) needed help in this regard, it is the present. That minister shares responsibility for agricultural policy with the mortician who is trying to bury PFRA, bury our transportation system, and bury the farmers of western Canada. Today he has been getting help from the Conservatives, particularly Conservatives coming from western
Agriculture
Canada. It seems to me that the minister's seat mate is trying to fight him. Also, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott) has not the faintest notion of the role of marketing legislation, and I suggest that he possesses no information which would lead him to conclude that marketing legislation is detrimental for the consumer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext: Hogwash!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That minister has hired a number of people of the Beryl Plumptre kind who are out to hang somebody. It seems that the person they are out to hang is the farmer.
Conservative members of this House should remember that in Ontario a Conservative government has been in power a long time. In Ontario we have more than 80 farm marketing boards, and I hear that the Davis government will not eliminate any one of them. I suggest that members of the Conservative party should come forward into the present century and look seriously at marketing legislation. No particular piece of marketing legislation is the full answer, for every commodity needs to be governed by a different type of marketing legislation.
Instead of fighting the Minister of Agriculture who has a knife in his back from his seatmate, and a knife in his back from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, he should be getting the support of all members of this House. In my opinion he has been doing his best to try to help the farmer. Hon. members can give that support by supporting the amendment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-AGRICULTURAL POLICIES AND PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the time remaining I would like to add to the remarks of the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters) with regard to the amendment. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) tried to make a speech about R. B. Bennett. That is as far as his thinking has gone. The whole principle of orderly marketing has been asked for by farm organizations since the early thirties.
The hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) says he cannot support the amendment because he wants producer-controlled marketing boards. I advise hon. members that we left out the words "producer-controlled" because that has been in the CCF-NDP policy since 1934. We felt that if we put the words "producer-controlled" in the amendment, the Conservatives would not vote for it.
I am glad to hear the hon. member for Moose Jaw, speaking on behalf of his party, say that they are in favour of producer-controlled marketing boards which, by the way, is the same as the amendment reads, "collective strength". The hon. member said he will vote against the amendment. If ever there was a classic case of talking out of both sides of your mouth and out of your top end and bottom end, this is it. The hon. member is against orderly marketing but in favour of producer-controlled marketing boards. I do not know out of which end he is talking. He must be talking out of both ends at the same time.

May 3, 1977
Agriculture
As the hon. member for Timiskaming said, when the PFRA was under the Minister of Agriculture, the Tories screamed bloody murder to have it taken away from him. By that time Jimmy Gardiner had fired all the Tories and hired a whole bunch of Liberals. Now they want it back under the Minister of Agriculture. I do not know what makes them think there would be any difference under one Liberal minister or another. It is not what they are doing but how they are doing it that bothers the Tories.
The fact that the official opposition wants to oppose this amendment lines them up with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) and the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Abbott). They are against orderly marketing.
